subsubtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF DOLLAR VALUE BY CHARTERED BANKS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter which is extremely important and weighs heavily on the Canadian economy.
Since the PQ government was elected in Quebec, Canadian speculators on the international foreign exchange market in Toronto, who are executives of the Canadian Bankers' Association, are taking advantage of that election to lower as they please the value of the Canadian dollar for the benefit of manipulators within the Canadian Bankers' Association, since only banks can determine and control the value of the Canadian dollar on the international foreign exchange market. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That a committee of the House be immediately instructed to look into and investigate that matter and to give the Bank of Canada exclusive control over the value of the Canadian dollar in terms of foreign currency, since the Bank of Canada is quite unaware of the secret manipulation conducted by private banks, through their association in Toronto, as they alone determine that value every day.

subsubtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF CABINET OF USE OF AGENTS-ACTION TO ENSURE FEES PROPERLY USED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. Yesterday, Mr. W. A. Bradshaw informed the public accounts committee of this House that on June 11, 1973 Mr. Lome Gray, who was then president of AECL, told the cabinet committee on government operations that a substantial agent's fee would be involved in the sale of a nuclear reactor to South Korea. In view of this evidence that the cabinet knew about this three years ago, would the Prime Minister tell the House what action he took to make certain that none of these agent's fees were going to be used in a way that might be repugnant to the moral standards of the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF CABINET OF USE OF AGENTS-ACTION TO ENSURE FEES PROPERLY USED
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat unusual to report what went on in cabinet, but in the circumstances I am prepared to indicate my knowledge of the matter. This was drawn to my attention. It was discussed with some of my colleagues and it appears that Mr. Gray, head of AECL, did mention this $500 million contract, that it would involve using an agent, that no authorization was sought. It was just a statement of reality and my colleagues took note of it but made no further comment or had no further discussion of it.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY IN SETTING MORAL STANDARDS FOR OPERATION OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, given the peculiar relationship that exists between Crown corporations and the government, and the fact that the government has set up Crown corporations to be independent of government, does the Prime Minister and his cabinet take the position that this relationship means the government and parliament have no responsibility in setting the moral standards and practices that these corporations operate within? In other words, my question is, what is the Prime Minister's definition of responsibility in setting the ethical and moral standards of Crown corporations? Is there any, or are they so far removed from the government that the government has no role to play whatsoever?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY IN SETTING MORAL STANDARDS FOR OPERATION OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows the legislation which sets up Crown corporations deliberately sets them up at arm's length from the government, so we have no direct power to command, intervene or survey the day to day operations. On a yearly basis we do look at their budgets. The question is raised as to whether or not the government should have, under some new legislation, a more direct power to intervene and direct, but this will be discussed in due course. This does not mean we are indifferent to the legal or moral behaviour of Crown corporations. When I issued the conflict of interest guidelines, for instance, I
Oral Questions
made them applicable to all members of my cabinet. In the case of Crown corporations, I sent them copies and suggested they follow certain procedures. We do not have any way of knowing on a day to day basis what their procedures are, but, I repeat, when they have very important budgetary problems they do come to cabinet where they are discussed.

subsubtopic: DATE OF CABINET MINUTE CONCERNING USE OF AGENTS- RELATIONSHIP IN TIME TO LETTER FROM MR. HENDERSON TO PRIME MINISTER

It is because it was a very large budgetary matter which was being dealt with that AECL came before cabinet to indicate what it was doing. One of the things it said it was doing was that it would have to hire an agent, I believe in South'Korea or elsewhere, in order to help us with this deal. I must point out to the House that just about everything that is sold abroad by Canadians, either by Crown corporations or private citizens, is sold through agents. So there is nothing unusual about that. When we sell powdered milk or skim milk we do it through an agent. When we sell wheat we do it through an agent. When

we sell material goods we do it through an agent. So, there are agents all the time, Mr. Speaker, and the House should not think the fact of the existence of agents is unusual.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENT TO SECTIONS CONCERNING PORNOGRAPHY AND OBSCENITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. In view of the public campaign of the Archbishop of Toronto, Archbishop Pocock, and also the open letter from him this morning to the citizens of this country which appears in the press, which is merely another indication of the very real concern not only of church leaders but also of community leaders regarding the laws in this country respecting pornography and obscenity and the very great difficulty which provincial officials and law enforcement agencies are having in respect of the enforcement of the existing laws relating to pornography and obscenity, I wonder if the minister would inform us if he is giving any consideration whatsoever to revising the definition sections of our laws relating to those two subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENT TO SECTIONS CONCERNING PORNOGRAPHY AND OBSCENITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the moment I am not considering any amendments to the law or making any recommendations. The Law Reform Commission has done considerable work in this area and will be doing more with regard to what the law should say.
However, I share the concern which has been expressed by the archbishop and which has been expressed to me by a number of provincial attorneys general. We discussed the matter of pornography at our June meeting, both in terms of more effective prosecutions under the Criminal Code which, of course, is their responsibility, and also, if possible, more effective measures at the federal level under the Customs Act. Since that meeting I have had a number of meetings on the subject with my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to assure that there is the most effective possible liaison between customs officials, both in the field and at the head office and to ensure that there are proper procedures for liaison by which provincial police forces and attorneys general may communicate to the customs officers their knowledge of undesirable material which is coming into the country so that customs officers can be as effective as possible in keeping it out.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. It arises out of earlier answers he gave in the House. Since the Prime Minister received a letter from Mr. Henderson, the former Auditor General, in March 1973 outlining very serious concern on his part about the financial operations of a particular Crown corporation and since evidence was provided to a committee of the House yesterday showing that cabinet in June approved the hiring of an agent with no ceiling on the money to be spent and no other guidelines and substantial amounts of money were spent to promote the sale of a CAN DU reactor, does the Prime Minister not believe that the information the Auditor General provided to him in March ought to have been relevant to the cabinet decision in June?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: RELEVANCE OF LETTER FROM MR. HENDERSON TO DECISION ON AGENT FOR ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. They were on completely different subjects. Mr. Henderson's letter does not talk about any agent. It does not talk about any illegality. It just talks about accounting practices which are approved by some auditors and disapproved by him, practices of a Crown corporation, Polysar, the books of which he himself audited and signed the audit as correct. He was concerned with a particular practice, which was properly brought to my attention and upon which I took action, which the House knows.
The subsequent meeting-if the hon. member says it was in June, it was June-had to do with one of the contracts which another Crown corporation was seeking to obtain with one of the several countries where we had been trying to sell the
Privilege-Mr. Walter Baker
CANDU reactor. I do not see any direct relationship between them. I repeat what I have said earlier: most of what is sold by Canada abroad is sold through agents. Members on the other side, I would hope, take no exception to the use of agents. The only relevant matter is whether their actions are illegal or immoral. I made it clear that the government takes the position that their actions should be both legal and moral.

subsubtopic: RELEVANCE OF LETTER FROM MR. HENDERSON TO DECISION ON AGENT FOR ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Henderson categorically rejects the view presented by the Prime Minister that what he was concerned about was just a question of accounting practices. Rather, the accounting practices gave rise to these moral issues. Given this judgment by Mr. Henderson, with regard to the behaviour of one Crown corporation, does the Prime Minister not think it would have been proper, the matter having been brought to his attention, not only to have referred the letter to the President of the Treasury Board for action but to have followed through to ascertain whether other Crown corporations were engaging in similar trade practices, possibly involving improper behaviour?

subsubtopic: RELEVANCE OF LETTER FROM MR. HENDERSON TO DECISION ON AGENT FOR ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
I must disagree with the hon. member when he says the concern of the former auditor general was with the morality of the practice. There is no question of morality in his letter, no indication that there might be anything immoral. His concern is about a contingent liability; other auditors say there is no contingent liability. Mr. Henderson in his letter, says:
The reason I have not insisted upon disclosure etc. of this contingent liability was that to have done so would, in my view, have been contrary to the best interests of Polymer as a multi-national corporation trading in a highly competitive field in world markets.
He is obviously concerned about what happened over there. He is explaining why he does not bring it out publicly. The reason is that he did not want to damage Canada commercially. This was a deal involving half a billion dollars and, I suppose, thousands of jobs for Canadians. If the Auditor General had thought action was being taken immorally on behalf of Canadians, no doubt he would have brought it to the attention of parliament or refused to sign the audit of the books of Polysar, which he did sign.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday an issue arose in the House in response to a question asked by me. The exchange began as recorded on pages 1592 and 1593 of Hansard. I gave notice to the Chair yesterday of my intention to raise a question of privilege today. I do so on the understanding that any question which I raise cannot affect me in a special capacity but it must affect all members of the House and it is my respectful submission to you, sir, that this did.
The matter was alluded to again in the last question asked by the leader of the New Democratic Party, but it all arose out of an unusual set of circumstances which I think I should be

December 3, 1976
Privilege-Mr. Walter Baker
allowed to develop briefly. It arose because of an incident which occurred in the House on November 26, 1976, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tabled certain documents which dealt with invoicing practices. One of those documents was a letter to the Prime Minister from the former auditor general dated March 22, 1973, and another important document related to is the Prime Minister's letter, also part of the House record, which was dated March 27, 1973.
The issue, of course, is an accusation that members on this side are smuggling lies and falsehoods into the debate. I raise the matter of the importance of the letter because of the fact that there was a special arrangement made with the Prime Minister so that he himself could put on the record that which he alludes to and accuses us of smuggling in as lies and falsehoods.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I refer hon. members and Your Honour to the proceedings of that day. I respectfully suggest that what happened to cause the Prime Minister to bring about his outburst yesterday was the fact that he is now reaping the bitter fruits of that which he seeded in this House on November 26.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I am not suggesting that the Prime Minister acted improperly on that occasion. I think he acted quite properly, and said so at the time. The point at issue is not whether the practice which was alluded to in the letter of the auditor general and which was alluded to in the response of the Prime Minister in his letter to the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury) is legal or illegal. That is not the issue, and that judgment will be made somewhere else. The point is not whether the particular actions referred to are moral or immoral; that judgment is already being made somewhere else outside this chamber. The point is not even the notable distinction between the Prime Minister and his Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien). The Prime Minister says there are ethics governing Crown corporations in their relationships with foreigners; there are guidelines. On the other hand, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce advances the bedroom theory, as he did the other day in debate. The prime issue is a simple one. It is whether any member of this House can call another member of this House a liar.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Nobody did.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order, please. I should like to be able to give my undivided attention to all the participants in this discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The issue is whether any member can call an her member, or members generally, directly or indirectly, a liar. It makes no difference whether the accuser is a backbencher or whether he is a prime minister. All the precedents say the answer is clearly

no, whether the accusation is made directly or whether it is made indirectly or even if it is made hypothetically, as might perhaps be argued in this case. Nor is it sufficient to say that the Prime Minister might have acted beneath the dignity of his office. That is no answer because it would merely be stating the obvious. Yesterday, as recorded at page 1593 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
However, it would be helpful if in the meantime members opposite did not smuggle in lies and falsehoods.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: That is supposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Those who examine the record will note that I immediately objected and asked the Prime Minister for a retraction, in keeping with the way in which such matters have been dealt with in the past. I do not believe any serious argument can be made to suggest that the remark was anything but unparliamentary. Citation 151 of Beauchesne's states that among the expressions which are clearly unparliamentary are those containing charges of uttering deliberate falsehoods. When the issue arose on May 28, 1973, Mr. Speaker Lamoureux stated, as reported at page 4154 of Hansard for that day:
The hon. member confirms that he knows he has no right to accuse another member, whether he is a member on the other side of the House, a member of the government or on his own side of the House, of lying. 1 even hesitate to use the word. I would hope that in accordance with the long tradition of parliament the hon. member will co-operate with the Chair and not use language which is clearly unparliamentary.
For over 100 years this has formed the basis of a rule which is accepted by all hon. members. I think we set a very bad example to other parliamentary institutions in this country at all levels of government if the senior House in Canada does not conform to the long established rules of parliamentary debate.
Some hon. members have suggested-indeed, it was even suggested this morning in interjections across the floor-that the Prime Minister may have saved himself by the words "it would be helpful if in the meantime", used as a prefix to what he said and to which I refer as unparliamentary. If they take that view, then they have ignored citation 154(2) of Beauchesne's, which provides:
Words may not be used hypothetically, or conditionally, if they are plainly intended to convey a direct imputation. Putting a hypothetical case is not the way to evade what would be in itself disorderly.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, that citation is directly applicable to this case. In requesting that the Prime Minister withdraw the words he used yesterday, I wish to refer to words used by the former member for Verdun in connection with words used by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) which were ruled unparliamentary, and as a consequence the hon. member for York-Simcoe acted quite properly and withdrew them. The then member for Verdun said on that occasion:
-I hope the hon. gentleman, who has shown that he is basically a House of Commons man, will understand that some of these rules to which we seem to over-react are really to make the House of Commons work as it should, which is the concern of most of us. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal put it the other day, democracy depends on this House of Commons and the House of Commons depends on certain basic rules which may look rather silly but in the general context of things make the difference between this House operating and not operating.
December 3, 1976

Later, the then member for Verdun said:
Because this is a civilized chamber in which there are civilized people, members usually stand up, swallow their pride and apologize.
I hope the Prime Minister will be guided by those words of his former colleague, Mr. Speaker.

-it would be helpful if in the meantime members opposite did not smuggle in lies and falsehoods.
I read that, Mr. Speaker, as a wish, as an expectation.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Maybe it is an unrealistic hope, too, but that is what I read into those words. I do not read them as an accusation. If the hon. member opposite, any of his colleagues, or Your Honour, reads them as an accusation, then I want to withdraw them as an accusation.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I am sorry I did not catch your eye, Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of orders-I was answering a question from the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent)-and had I done so perhaps I could have saved the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton the need to make the statement that he did. But his having made it, I want to make one of my own. I would say there is no accusation intended there, and to the extent that there is one contained in the words, it is withdrawn. But there is an accusation which is very clearly made at the top of that same page and to which the hon. member does not take offence. I say this:
-the hon. member has smuggled into his question an allegation that is false and erroneous.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that these words are not unparliamentary and that I can use them, but that the other allegation of "lying" is unparliamentary. I do not want to make much of the words that are used, but last night I did look up the Dictionary of Canadian English by W. J. Gage, Toronto, 1967. All of these words appear to be synonomous: "false, falsehood, lie, false statement"-

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: "Liberal".

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member opposite did, I would ask Your Honour whether that is not at least an indirect statement that we are lying and it should be withdrawn. But I did accuse the hon. member of having smuggled into his question an allegation that was false and erroneous. What was that allegation, Mr. Speaker? At page 1592 the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton stated the following:
I wonder if he can advise the House whether those guidelines condone the practice which has been admitted by the head of the government, the practice of issuing inflated invoices by Crown corporations-
Privilege-Mr. Walter Baker
That is not only false and erroneous; it is a grave accusation which is false and erroneous.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
It is the accusation that there is a practice of issuing inflated invoices and that I admitted I knew of that practice. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that that is at the heart of the debate which has been going on for the past week or so in this House and in the country. I have established quite clearly that the only knowledge I had of inflated invoices was in one letter, which was followed by action which the House will be free to judge but which, in my mind, cleared up the matter, at least to the extent that there is a contradiction between two auditors. The matter has now been referred, quite properly, to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.
The point that I make, Mr. Speaker, is that the member for Grenville-Carleton made a false statement. Did he know that it was false? Only he can say if he knew it was false. If he knew it to be false, that is the dictionary definition of a lie. I assume, very gladly and openly, that he did not know it to be false but that he used it, as the expression goes, in the cut and thrust of debate. He was asking the question in the heated atmosphere of the House of Commons: he did not know it to be false. But if he did make a false and erroneous statement in a very serious accusation, I suggest that he owes me an apology.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Words are used all the time, Mr. Speaker, and I must say, sitting on these benches on this side of the House, I am not overly sensitive to them. I believe that the number of times I have asked hon. members opposite to withdraw has been very few indeed. Once or twice in a period of ten years I have drawn such a thing to Your Honour's attention, and that must be the maximum number of times. I think every member knows that day in and day out things are hurled across this aisle which are meant to offend, at least in a superficial way. I have heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) constantly come back with the line that the government should come clean, that the Prime Minister has not come clean, and so on. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, there is not much difference between that and saying that I am hiding something, that I am lying. But I do not take objection to it every time it happens.
I just want to make my point, that if the hon. member does not apologize, knowing that he made a grave accusation which is false, one must conclude that he wants that falsehood to stand; in other words, that he made that falsehood knowingly and I think that is the definition of a lie. I indicated, Mr. Speaker, that I am convinced the hon. member opposite did not know he was making a falsehood and did not do it knowingly. Therefore, I suggest he owes me an apology.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to thank the Prime Minister for the unconditional withdrawal,

December 3, 1976
Privilege-Mr. Walter Baker
in the first part of his interjection, regarding the documents and the statement he made yesterday. I think it should be noted that it was unconditional. He went on to say that if I knew those words to be false, then 1 owe him an apology. Let me say that in making any statement I made in the House, I relied on the documents that were filed by the Prime Minister and I think the written documents have to stand on their own words.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: You are a weak man.

I think it is important that the House and the Prime Minister understand that basis. On page 2 of his letter to Mr. Drury of March 27, 1973, the Prime Minister said:
Perhaps the right course would be for the appropriate minister, on behalf of the government, to draw this-
That is the practice referred to by Mr. Henderson.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER

-to draw this to the attention of the management of Polymer and CDC and express the hope that they will give serious consideration to the question whether any modification in the practices of Polymer in its trading arrangements is required.
Let me say this to the Prime Minister directly, through you, Mr. Speaker: when I read that document of March 22, 1973, I understood that the Prime Minister was accepting the words of the auditor general of Canada at that time when he stated the following:
-this arises from the subsidiary's practice of invoicing certain European customers, by agreement, at inflated prices, with the difference being remitted to the customers or their representatives in cash in Switzerland or placed in numbered Swiss bank accounts as directed.
Relying, as I am, on the records of the House, as I look at the record I do not feel I owe the Prime Minister an apology at all.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) was the first to raise this question of privilege yesterday. I cannot but conclude that the intervention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), whether or not the technical language was unparliamentary, and I must say that 1 agree with the interpretation-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-LANGUAGE USED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Order, please. I do not really see how I can entertain further discussion on a matter that has been conclud-

ed. When it was suggested that unparliamentary language was used yesterday, I did hear the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants develop his argument, and it is as a result of his having raised the point that it has come to the fore today.
The argument that was put forward by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants yesterday was that the use of the words "lies" and "falsehood" constituted unparliamentary language. It is always difficult for the Chair to have to decide on the interpretation of language. The clear precedent of the past is that even though there are always shades of meaning which tend to excuse the use of such language, when such language was used in the past it was found to be unparliamentary, and rather than getting into an interpretation of shades of meaning it is a safer course to take it as a danger signal and when that kind of language is used it must be withdrawn. The Prime Minister has conceded that point and has withdrawn the language. In my view, that puts an absolute and final conclusion to the question of privilege.
The next question raised was a matter of disagreement and not a question of procedure. It was not a matter raised as a question of privilege. It is, rather, a subject of interpretation as to whether the Prime Minister has, or has not, made an admission. The Prime Minister rejected that position in his intervention and the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) reiterated it. That is a disagreement between two members as to the interpretation that ought to be placed on the letters or the language suggested by the hon. member. As everyone will realize, there is a disagreement as to that interpretation and it constitutes a matter of debate, not a question of procedure in any way.
In so far as the procedural question is concerned, again I suggest that the Prime Minister, in withdrawing the words, has put a conclusion to it which certainly satisfies the Chair and, it seems to me, should satisfy all members of the House.

speechtext:
That this House condemns the central government for threatening the provinces with a unilaterally imposed patriation of a constitution which is obsolete and no longer responds to the aspirations of Canadians, rather than, as it should, leaving to the provinces the task of drafting a new constitution.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to thank the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada for this opportunity to introduce in the House a most important motion for the future of Canada, especially in the light of the current constitutional situation, due to the outcome of the November 15, 1976 provincial elections in Quebec, where the elected party's platform included a possible referendum within two years on the question of whether or not the people of Quebec want to remain in the Canadian confederation.
In view of the importance of the election of the Parti Quebecois as the government of Quebec and in view of the future of Canada, it is urgent that we deal with this question in all seriousness. Since the Fathers of Confederation took very seriously the future of Canada, it should be dealt with all the more seriously today when the future as well as the past of our country are threatened.
Many very important questions come to mind. What is our constitutional past? What is our constitutional future? Do we have a constitution? A real one? What is it? When was it agreed on? By whom? Where is it? Should we patriate it if we have one or should we develop a new one? If so, who should do that? How are we to do it? What should be included in it?
In order to give appropriate answers to all those questions, we have to go over the constitutional history of our country to find out where we stand and what we have to do, taking into account past and present circumstances so that we may plan a better future for our country and prevent, if possible, its break-up, because our ancestors put all their hopes in the future of Canada.
On February 5, 1841, the Union Act of Lower and Upper Canada united Quebec and Ontario. This union was based on

the principle of parliamentary equality of both provinces until the population of Upper Canada, which was Ontario, was almost equal to that of Lower Canada, which was Quebec. This union was then quite satisfactory. But when the population of Upper Canada clearly exceeded that of Lower Canada, Upper Canada began to ask for a better representation of its population. Facing this unsatisfactory situation, the Conservative member for Sherbrooke, Mr. Alexander Galt, then said on July 6, 1858 that unless a confederation was created, Canada would be swallowed by the United States. Thus Mr. Galt was the first member to request his party to introduce a confedera-tive project within the electoral program of the government party. Mr. Galt, who was then Minister of Finance, rejected the governor's invitation to form the government. Cartier had this honour but Galt had convinced him of the value of his project to set up a confederation. So, on September 1, 1843, the Honourable John A. Macdonald, the future Prime Minister of the Canadian Confederation in 1867, married his cousin, Miss Isabelle Clark. They had two sons and in the fall of 1858, Cartier, Galt and John Ross went to England to submit their project to set up a Confederation of Canada drafted by Galt. This project met with polite indifference on the part of .England because Great Britain had by then lost practically all interest in Canada. On September 1, 1864, a conference to promote a federal union was held in Charlottetown. This meeting was adjourned to October 10, 1864 in Quebec City where all the provinces were represented. In Quebec City, on October 10, 1864, the respective merits of a legislative union, a confederation or a federal union were discussed. The first resolution of this important conference reads as follows, and I quote:

Whereas the best interests and present and future prosperity of British North America will be promoted by a Federal Union under the Crown-

And on March 13, 1865, those resolutions were ratified by both Quebec and Ontario legislatures and accepted by the Maritime provinces in 1866. On December 3, 1866, Canadian delegates arrived in London with their project on a federal union. Their conference opened on December 4, 1866 to terminate on December 24, 1866, Christmas Eve. Sir John A. Macdonald acted as chairman for the Canadian delegation. At the opening of the morning session on December 4, Canadian delegates who were meeting at the Westminster Palace Hotel to draft a bill concerning resolutions passed in Quebec were handed another bill which had been drafted by Lord Thring, parliamentary adviser to the British treasury, upon instructions from Lord Carnarvon, the Secretary of State for Colonial Affairs.
Canadian delegates did not appreciate at all the early interference of the Colonial Office in London. They were told that the bill drafted by the Colonial Office was designed only to help them in their deliberations, to guide them and not to influence them. On the front page of the bill which had been drafted and printed by the Colonial Office in London, one can read the following and I quote:
December 3, 1976

The union of the colonies and or the government of the United Colony. Whereas the union of the British North American colonies for purposes of government and legislation would be attended with great benefits to the colonies and be conducive to the interests of the United Kingdom.
[ Translation]
And clause 1 of the bill reads as follows:

This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1967. [Translation]
On the right hand side of the copy of the bill of the Colonial Office in London that Sir John A. Macdonald had been given and that can be found at the National Archives, one can see what Sir John A. Macdonald wrote in his own hand to correct the bill prepared by the Colonial Office in London and showing clearly among other things the disagreement of the Canadian delegation with the draft bill prepared by the Colonial Office in London. These corrections read as follows, and 1 quote:

Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to form a federal union for the purposes of government and legislation based on the principles of the British constitution-

Consequently, the purpose of the British North America Act that was proposed by London was to unite the colonies in a Dominion while the purpose of the bill that the Canadian delegation was preparing went along the lines of the resolutions passed in Quebec City to unite the provinces in a federal union somewhat like the Union Act that had united Lower and Upper Canada.
Federal union meant complete and total freedom of the provinces; federal meant freedom of choice; Dominion means domination over the colonies. In fact, England was not ready in 1866 to give sovereign status to its colonies, particularly the provinces of Canada, because of the situation that existed in 1865 between the Canadian provinces at that time and the United States that had broken away from England in 1776.
Several reasons gave England cause to fear annexation of the Canadian provinces by the United States in 1866. Among others, on July 2, 1866, exactly five months after the Canadian delegation had been to London, the American banks put before Congress a bill asking it to welcome the Canadian provinces as American states. So the Canadian delegates prepared their bill for a federal union from December 4 to December 24, 1866, and then waited impatiently for the bill that meant so much to them to be assented to, because they had gone to London to fight for the federal union of the provinces which would have given them full sovereignty or national independence since they had been strongly influenced by the American independence that was already more than 90 years old. Furthermore England no longer seemed interested in Canada because it had done very little for it for a long time.
The Constitution
While there was some lobbying by Canadians towards a federal union and the Colonial Office was planning some strategy to have the British North America Act passed, the chairman of the Canadian delegation, John A. Macdonald, who was however totally trusted by Canadian delegates, was very seriously courting Miss Suzan Agnes Bernard, Colonel Montague Bernard's sister, secretary to the Canadian delegation in London. That position was cleverly entrusted by Lord Carnarvon, the Secretary of State for Colonial Affairs. Meanwhile the sentimental negotiations of John A. Macdonald were making better progress than the constitutional negotiations of the federal union of the Canadian provinces. Instead of achieving that union, John A. Macdonald achieved the marital union with Miss Suzan Bernard on February 16, 1867. John A. Macdonald had met his future wife, Miss Suzan Bernard, in Toronto in 1856 when she was staying at Lake Simcoe, Ontario.
On December 28, 1857, Mrs. Macdonald, his first wife, died, and in September 1865, Miss Suzan Agnes Bernard and her mother decided to move to London where her brother, Colonel Montague Bernard, was already living. It was a year later, in December 1866, during the Canadian delegation conference in London, that John A. Macdonald met again Miss Bernard with whom he had remained on friendly terms after her departure from Canada and following their first meeting in 1856, particularly due to Miss Bernard's brother, Colonel Montague Bernard who had been John A. Macdonald's private secretary when he lived in Canada. In 1866, he was professor of international law at Oxford University in London and, at the same time, secretary of the Canadian delegation conference in London. The wedding of John A. Macdonald and Miss Bernard took place in St. George's church, Hanover Square, in London, at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, on February 16, 1867. At half-past twelve on the same day, John A. Macdonald and his intended wife were honoured with a special audience with Her Majesty the Queen Victoria. They were accompanied by Cartier, Galt, Tupper and Tilley, and Her Majesty the Queen was attended by Princess Louise and Lord Carnarvon, Colonial Secretary of State, who had arranged the protocol in every detail to please the bride and the bridegroom, the most important member of the Canadian delegation who was seeking from London the federal union of the provinces, which Lord Carnarvon would not accept under any circumstances.
England was resorting to diplomacy and strategy, while the Canadians naively thought they were sincere and truthful. Macdonald came in first to meet Her Majesty, and then the other parliamentarians followed one after the other. They had never met Her Majesty before. They were delighted and the Queen offered the highest praise to Macdonald and his colleagues. She hardly mentioned the purpose of the Canadian delegation's visit to London, but she said to John A. Macdonald:

It is a very important measure and you have always exhibited so much loyalty.

December 3, 1976
The Constitution

Lord Carnarvon stayed throughout the meeting with the Queen, John A. Macdonald and all the other Canadian delegates.
The day following the wedding reception which was held at the Westminster Palace Elotel, the very day when the Canadian delegates conference took place, Colonel Montague Bernard, John A. Macdonald's new brother-in-law and former private secretary in Canada, conveyed him a message from Lord Carnarvon, namely that the bridegroom would be appointed to the very important office of Privy Councillor in London, but that there were a small technical problem to be settled before that important appointment.
That technicality, as explained by a teacher of international law, was readily understood by John A. Macdonald: his appointment to the Privy Council in London would be impossible without his accepting the British North America Act. Now, a few days later, March 27, 1867, only one month after the marriage of John A. Macdonald, Queen Victoria signed the British North America Act. By accepting this act, John A. Macdonald legalized in advance the possibility that he might become a member of the Privy Council of London and Her Majesty, as he had been promised.

Because before 1867, or before the acceptance of the British North America Act, no right hon. member of Her Majesty's Privy Council could sit in the legislature, and after the British North America Act of 1867, John A. Macdonald could sit, as he did, as a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council of England in Canada. By the promise of eventually becoming a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council, John A. Macdonald was compelled to take orders from them, and as prime minister of Canada he was appointed as a member of the High Commission to the United States to settle the terms of the Treaty of Washington with his brother-in-law, the Right Hon. Montague Bernard, on May 8, 1871.

History never told us why John A. Macdonald's brother-inlaw was also appointed to the London Privy Council on that date. After having served well the British Crown as a loyal British subject, and because he had not caused any problems for England with the Federal Union Act, and because of the very great facility with which he understood the message of Queen Victoria on his wedding day, and for having accepted the British North America Act, as promised he was appointed to the London Privy Council in July, 1872, and was sworn in at the St. James court in London.
And as the British North America Act stipulates-
The Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald could sit as the sole representative of the British government in Canada. This has been possible only through the acceptance of the British North America Act.

On February 19, 1867, just three days after John A. Macdonald's wedding and the commitment made by his brother-inlaw that he would eventually become a member of the Privy Council in London, the private bill for the British North America Act that had been drafted by the Colonial Office was introduced in the House of Lords by Lord Carnarvon, the Secretary of State for Colonial Affairs, the chief of Colonel Montagu Bernard, new brother-in-law of John A. Macdonald and appointed by him secretary of the Canadian delegates in London.
The Canadian delegation that went to London to obtain Canadian sovereignty through a federal union, came back very disappointed with the official status of colony conferred by the British North America Act. But with his great power of persuasion, the chairman John A. Macdonald, convinced the majority of delegates that it was a good compromise, while his colleagues who had visited the queen with Macdonald were unsatisfied and considered the British North America Act as a complete capitulation. As for John A. Macdonald, while he had not achieved the federal union of the provinces, he had nevertheless tied a bound of matrimony and was promised, as a wedding gift, a seat in Her Majesty's Privy Council, to which he was indeed appointed in 1872.
Having stressed the negotiations, diplomacy, strategy and extra-parliamentary relations which paved the way for the British North America Act, I would now like to comment on the funny way with which the London Parliament dealt with this bill, because at the time of the first reading they did not discuss the preamble of the bill but rather the Quebec resolutions which were not even printed in the bill but merely attached to it.
At the time of the second reading, that is February 27, 1867, the Quebec resolutions were indeed printed but the preamble of the first reading had been substituted between the first reading and the printing of the bill for its second reading. This parliamentary process raised the protests of Mr. Had-field, member of the British House of Commons, as reported in the British Commons proceedings of the 26, 27 and 28 of February, 1867.
Mr. Speaker, in order to demonstrate the kind of wheeling and dealing which surrounded the passing of the bill, I would like to quote a statement by Sir John Bourinot in Canada: [English]
In "Canada under British Rule," chapter 8, page 215, he says that it is interesting to know that in the original draft of the bill the united provinces were called "the kingdom of Canada", but when it came eventually before parliament, they were designated as the Dominion of Canada, and the writer had it from Sir John A. Macdonald himself that this amendment did not emanate from the colonial delegates but from the imperial ministry. This act was drafted by the law officers of the Crown attached to the Colonial Office of which Lord Carnarvon was chairman. I quote Sir Frederick Rogers, undersecretary for the colonies, as follows:

December 3, 1976

They held many meetings at which 1 was always present. Lord Carnarvon was in the chair, and I was rather disappointed in the power of presidency.
That is taken from "Lord Blachford's Letters", page 301. The law officers of the Crown drafted the bill to guide the delegates, the title of which read, "The Union of British North American Colonies and for the Government of the United Colonies". The preamble was as follows:
Whereas the union of the British North American colonies for the purpose of government and legislation would be attended with great benefits to the colonies and be conductive to the interests of the United Kingdom.
This was the desire of the Colonial Office, and it appears that it prevailed over the desire of the provinces, which was as follows:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to form a federal union under the British Crown for the purpose of government and legislation based upon the principles of the British constitution.
Why was Lord Carnarvon chairman of the delegates from Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick? Was this not a violation of natural laws? If the British North America Act contained in some measure the desire expressed by the provinces, would it not have been simply a matter of common courtesy on the part of the noble lord who was chairman of the delegates from Canada and who introduced the bill in the House of Lords at least to have returned a copy of the act for the consideration and consent of the local legislature?
The British North America Act which was enacted by the imperial parliament was not the British North America Act our delegates desired. It did not conform with the Quebec resolutions. Instead of becoming a federal union, as the Quebec resolutions called for, Canada was demoted to the status of a colony under the name "dominion" which, according to the Interpretation Act enacted 22 years later, was defined as one colony. Had Canada become a federal union, an agreement between the provinces would necessarily have had to be signed and later ratified by the Canadian electorate. No such agreement was signed and the British North America Act has never been submitted to the Canadian electorate for its approval, without which there cannot be a legal constitution. It was not in order for the British North America Act in the form in which it was enacted to be ratified by the Canadian people because it was nothing but an ordinary imperial bill with which the imperial parliament alone had the authority. This parliament has always been a dominion parliament and not a federal parliament. Calling it federal will not make it such. A federal government can be created only by agreement among the provinces, and that agreement must be ratified by the electorate. This has not been done.
What reason, therefore, have we for calling this a federal parliament? Through the British North America Act the sovereignty of the Canadian people was withheld from them. Consequently, they were unable to federate. The British North America Act is not a constitution in the true sense of the word. It has been called a constitution and has been used as one, but that does not make it one. A federal constitution is an agreement between federating states, and it must be ratified by the people. The British North America Act is not, and cannot be,
The Constitution
a federal constitution. It was designed by the imperial authorities as a statute for the government of a colony, and obviously it cannot be used as the basis of an agreement for a federal union. Dr. Ollivier former joint law clerk of the House of Commons, at page 85 of the committee report on the British North America Act in 1935, said:
A confederation is a union of independent and sovereign states bound together by a pact or a treaty for the observance of certain conditions dependent upon the unanimous consent of the contracting parties who are free to withdraw from the union.
The definition indicates-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-PATRIATION OF CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Dr. Ollivier, former joint law clerk of the House of Commons, said at page 85 of the report on the British North America Act in 1935:
Confederation is a union of independent and sovereign states bound together by a pact or a treaty for the observance of certain conditions dependent upon the unanimous consent of the contracting parties who are free to withdraw from the union.
This definition indicates that the status of sovereignty must precede confederation and that a federal union can be consummated only by the mutual consent of contracting states adopting a constitution.
Mr. Speaker, from the evidence which I have thus far submitted, I draw the following conclusions: first, the provinces of Canada desired a federal union; second, the Quebec resolutions provided for a federal union; third, the bill drafted by the Canadian delegates at the London conference also provided for a federal union; fourth, the Colonial Office was not disposed to grant the provinces of Canada their request for a federal union; fifth, the British North America Act, enacted by the imperial parliament, carried out neither the spirit nor the terms of the Quebec resolutions; sixth, Canada did not become a federal union under the British North America Act but, rather, a united colony. The privilege of federating, therefore, was still a future privilege.
Seventh, the parliament of Canada did not become the government of Canada, much less a federal government. It became merely the central legislature of a united colony, a legislative body whose only power was that of aiding and advising the governor general as agent of the imperial parliament. Eight, the British North America Act, as enacted by the imperial parliament, was not a constitution but merely an act of the imperial parliament which united four colonies in Canada into one colony with the supreme authority still remaining in the hands of the British government.

December 3, 1976
The Constitution

Mr. Speaker, of all the debates held on the history of Canada, the constitutional debate seems to be recurring most often. Although the opinions which were voiced here are most shocking, they nevertheless reflect what I consider as the only truth. However, we should not believe they are unfounded revelations since they are shared and have been made public by people whose competence is well known such as Dr. Ollivi-er, Doctor of Laws and former law expert in the House of Commons, Dr. Scantland, former Secretary of State for External Affairs and Mr. Beauchesne, former clerk of the House of Commons, who appeared as witnesses before the Special Committee on the British North America Act of 1935. Further, the opinions voiced are similar to those expressed by Professor Roger Smith, an expert on constitutional matters and Mr. W. Kool, Member of Parliament for Jasper-Edson in the 40's.
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I am making today are the result of ten years of intensive research and are based on undeniable sources of work, research and competence. The British North America Act was nothing else than the recognition of a unified North American colony under the authority of the Imperial government in London. Moreover, this Act did not allow the formation of a government as such, but rather that of a Central Parliament and Provincial Legislatures subject to England. The statute of sovereign government would have given the provinces their sovereignty if the British Parliament had granted their request for a federal union.
But this sovereignty only remained a remote possibility because, by refusing to form a real confederation, the English Parliament denied the provinces the right to create:
A Union of Confederation of sovereign states created by treaty or by mutual adoption of a federal Constitution . ..
-according to the definition found in Mr. Bouvier's law dictionary.
It is therefore obvious that following the English refusal, Canada was not in 1867 a Confederation as requested in the Quebec resolutions, because the British North America Act should have been based on the Quebec and not the London conference. Indeed, while the Quebec resolutions contained 72 paragraphs, the British North America Act contains 147 paragraphs, that is more than twice as much.
Secondly, the so-called constitution of the British North America Act is not a contract between the provinces, since in 1867 no agreement had been reached among them. The most obvious evidence of that lies in the BNA Act having been amended six times between 1871 and 1918, namely in 1871, 1875, 1886, 1907, 1915 and 1918, five of which without the consent of or even consultation with the provinces.
This is indeed contrary to the concept of a contract or a confederative pact, as mentioned on page 59 of the Special Committee report on the British North America Act.

speechtext:
Thirdly, the British North America Act has never been either legal or valid as a Canadian constitution, because its preamble is wrong, there having been a change between two Parliamentary readings, as I demonstrated a while ago. Because of this procedural infringement, it is worthless as far as the constitution of Canada, a sovereign and independent state since 1931, is concerned.
Canada then has no constitution, since there is no certified copy in Canada to prove the agreement of the provinces. Although there was a central legislature, there was no centralized legal sovereign government in Canada following the signing of the British North America Act in 1867. At all events, the Statute of Westminster adopted on December 11, 1931 finally made Canada a sovereign country. Normally, Canada should have the right to change its constitution, if she had one, or to adopt a brand new one, by mutual agreement with the provinces, since it was to them that the new statute granted sovereignty.
Now this, and it is very important, Mr. Speaker, has not been allowed because section 7 of the Statute of Westminster stated that nothing in this Act shall be deemed to apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1930. Yet it would seem that were it not for this section, which however only applied to Canada since Australia and New Zealand were exempted from it, there would have been no federal government nor common constitution for the provinces, but they would rather have been fully sovereign and totally free to give themselves a constitution and to decide on which kind of central government they wanted.
And finally, to submit the whole thing to their citizens for approval or adoption. However, they were denied that most legitimate right to that unique and true independence, strictly because the then central Parliament in Ottawa wangled its way around the government in London and asked it to include Section 7 in the Statute of Westminster which gave it the right to keep such powers as it exercised since 1867, powers determined by the British North America Act.
Mr. Speaker, Section 7 is unconstitutional. Why? Because the government in London could, under no circumstances, without the consent of the provinces, transfer to Ottawa the power it held over the Canadian provinces, by including Section 7 in the Statute of Westminster.
The fact that this imposture resulted in the impossibility of changing the constitution on the one hand, and in the denial of the true sovereignty of the provinces on the other hand, did not seem to impress the central legislature of the time enough to make them hesitate before this supreme infamy. In view of those facts, Mr. Speaker, Canada's new status as sovereign state under the 1931 Statute of Westminster has never been submitted to the people for approval and consequently section
December 3, 1976

7 of this statute from which the federal government derives its present power-a government which still continues to submit us symbolically to the British Crown-is illegal and void. As a result, the Canadian provinces, which acquired their independence in 1931, do not have a constitution for they never voted on it. So the central government of Ottawa which, by constitutional pretention, takes its authority in section 7 of the Statute of Westminster, does not have any legal status because the parties to which the Statute of Westminster refers-the Canadian provinces-never did grant or give it such authority. In brief, Canada does not have any constitution. This explains why it is necessary to adopt one and to submit it to the people, as did Australia after the Statute of Westminster, and as suggested by Mr. Beauchesne and several other competent witnesses who appeared before the special committee on the British North America Act of 1935. The federal government has been governing this country for more than 40 years without any legal status because the newly independent provinces of 1931 never granted it any authority.
Through the Statutes of Westminster, the people of Canada and the provinces of Canada acquired their sovereignty. Since that time neither the provinces, by agreement, nor the people of Canada, by ratification, have delegated any of this sovereignty to a central government. The central government of a sovereign nation can acquire the power of disallowance, if such there be, only from the provinces which create and delegate authority to the central government. This has not been done in Canada. The Statutes of Westminster, in my opinion, now remove the obstacles to federation. By virtue of this act, the overlordship of the British people was relinquished and the people of Canada are now in full possession of their sovereignty. The provinces of Canada were given sovereign status in order that they might federate.
They could not federate without this status, but to date neither the provinces nor the people of Canada have acted upon this attainment of sovereign status. Legally, Canada is a state of anarchy and has been so since December 11, 1931. All power given to govern in Canada since the enactment of the Statutes of Westminster has resided with the provinces of Canada, and all power legally remains there until such time as the provinces sign an agreement and ratify a constitution whereby they delegate such powers as they desire upon a central government of their own creation.
Since December 11, 1971, the parliament of Canada has governed Canada on assumed power only. If we are to have a constitution, we must make one. We must do as Dr. Beauchesne suggested to the special committee on the British North America Act in 1935, when he suggested that we begin this new constitution by calling a constituent assembly of representatives from the provinces. This constituent assembly was to draft a constitution which would later be ratified by the people.
The Constitution
In the creating of this new constitution, provision can be made for its amendment. This would end once and for all the controvery that arises whenever an amendment to the British North America Act is contemplated. On page 125 of the report of the same committee Dr. Beauchesne had this to say:
The new constitution must leave nobody with a grievance. A spirit of conciliation should predominate. For these reasons, the task must be entrusted to an independent body in which all the elements of the country will be represented.
I, therefore, beg to suggest an imposing constituent assembly formed of eminent men coming from all parts of Canada. Provincial conferences attended by a few ministers meeting behind closed doors would hardly satisfy public opinion. The debate should be public. Again, as is said on page 129, whether our country should be changed from a dominion to a kingdom is also a subject which might be discussed. I would suggest that the country be called "The federated states of Canada".

Having enjoyed sovereignty since the Statute of Westminster, the provinces are the only ones that can proceed to a new distribution of powers. It is only through usurpation of powers that the federal government can even speak of a new sharing because it has been acting since 1931 as if it had a constitution. When the new Premier of Quebec, Mr. Rene Levesque, elected last November 15, will want to ask the population of Quebec whether or not it wishes to stay in confederation, he will be mistaken for Quebecers cannot be asked to opt out through a referendum since they were never so consulted to join it in the first place. In order to opt out, they had to opt in in the same way. Since the Statute of Westminster, Quebec and the other provinces are already separated because they are sovereign and if they still think they are part of the Canadian confederation, it is because they still believe in the myth of a constitution which still does not exist.
And when the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) says that he wants to patriate the constitution, he perpetuates a myth; without this, the existence of a constitution is impossible. So the federal government is powerless among sovereign provinces because if the provinces of Canada stopped believing in the myth of a so-called constitution tomorrow morning-I am concluding my speech, Mr. Speaker-and if they believed in their own sovereign power, our constitutional problem in Canada would immediately be 95 per cent solved.
Mr. Speaker, a federal council without any executive or financial power was established in Australia in 1885 by an act of parliament, and in 1891 there was a federal convention to consider the establishment of a new constitution for Australia. It was rejected but it became the basis for the federal convention of 1897 and 1898 which opened the way to a constitution and which was approved by a referendum in 1899 and ratified by an act of Parliament on July 9, 1900; this gave birth to the Commonwealth of Australia on January 1, 1901. Mr. Speaker, since then Australia has a true constitution. Just prove to me when such a procedure was followed in Canada to give the country a constitution which is truly Canadian.

An eighth attempt was made by prime minister Pearson in June 1964. A great deal of work was done at that time under the aegis of the then minister of justice, the Hon. Guy Favreau.
There appeared what, was later called the Fulton-Favreau formula, since it took up again in part the formula put forward in the early sixties by Mr. Fulton. But once again it failed.
A ninth attempt goes back to the federal-provincial conference of February 1968 which evolved into a permanent constitutional conference. This constitutional conference, as you know, lead to the Victoria charter which also failed to find a formula agreeable to all parties.
A tenth attempt was made in April 1975 when the Prime Minister P. E. Trudeau made his proposal. During a dinner with the provincial premiers in April 9, 1975, the Prime Minister of Canada asked that the British North America Act be patriated without delay, according to the amending formula agreed to in Victoria, as concerns those parts of the constitution that cannot be presently amended in Canada.
The Prime Minister expressed the opinion at that time that this should be done without re-opening for the moment any other important constitutional issue. He said at the time that we could deal with that later after developing an amending formula and especially after taking that most important step, namely patriating the constitution.
The Prime Minister of Canada drafted some proposals and sent them to the provincial premiers on April 19, 1975. He wrote among other things: "It would be beneficial to patriate the British North America Act shortly before the 1976 Olympic Games. It would be an ideal opportunity, he said in his letter, for Her Majesty to attend a special ceremony in Ottawa, with all the provincial premiers in attendance, and to put the final touch to the historical proceedings pertaining to our constitution." Now, we know the rest, the Queen came to Canada, and there was no patriation of the constitution.
In April 1976, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) again sent provincial premiers, not a provoking, threatening letter as was suggested today in the motion put forward by the Social Credit Party, but a letter offering the premiers three specific, well defined motions. The first one, the easiest, reads:
.. . that we should at least repatriate . ..
-the Canadian constitution.
... it would be possible ... to include a provision under which parts of the constitution that are now unamendable, could be amended with the unanimous consent of Parliament and legislative assemblies, until such time as a permanent formula can be found and established.
That was an option open to the provinces.
... a second option ... would be to include a provision allowing the establishment of a permanent and more flexible amendment formula.
And finally, a third option which was put forward would:
... include in the patriation formula the entire content of the proposed proclamation ...
The Constitution
-which was enclosed in the letter. And the Prime Minister said in conclusion:
... we would avail ourselves not only of the patriation and amendment formula but also of the other provisions which were progressively worked out during the discussions which have been held so far.
And God knows, Mr. Speaker, how many discussions and talks there were during the past 50 years in order to repatriate the Canadian constitution. Now, when the hon. member for Shefford says that the government of Canada, through its Prime Minister, threatens the provinces, I suggest it is nonsense and unwarranted to make such remarks. It is obvious that one of the major reasons for our failure is that the provincial premiers have failed to come to an agreement. As you know, a series of meetings were held following the Prime Minister's letter of last April. The first meeting was held in Ottawa in June, 1976 and attended by the Prime Minister of Canada and provincial premiers. It was followed by a meeting in Edmonton in early August, and another in Toronto last October, just a few weeks ago. And the same headlines still appear in the press. I quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail, which says:
10 PREMIERS STALLED AGAIN ON BN A TALKS
And this one was published in The Press:

speechtext: -at the request of provincial premiers. Here is another headline from the Quebec Soleil:

The real plain and basic matter is that the Canadian government would like to repatriate the Constitution; they would like this constitutional text to be here in Canada rather than in Great Britain but the problems we shall have to face remain the same-there must be unanimous agreement between all 10 provinces. Now, when the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) said in the second part of his motion that the government should give the provinces the opportunity to draft a new Constitution, I must disagree with that suggestion and remind him that indeed, there is a Canadian constitution which concerns the elected provincial representatives as well as federal representatives. I find it surprising and amazing that a federal member would have been led to believe that there is no Canadian constitution and to abdicate its responsibilities towards Parliament advocating that the provinces and not the Canadian parliament has capacity to amend the Canadian constitution.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.
The hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) on a point of order.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to put a question to the minister, I have based my whole speech not on some personal views, but on the statements of individuals
