with greater expertise than myself and the minister in constitutional matters. I am referring to Dr. Beauchesne and Dr. Ollivier and their evidence given in 1935 on the British North America Act in Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
I have no objection that the hon. member should not endorse the words he has previously quoted. In any event, talking about expertise, I would like to quote again Mr. Jean-Charles Bonenfant, who in his book which was published by Les Editions La Presse under the title "La Constitution", said on page 29, and I quote:
There is another solution that is sometimes advanced by some politicians when they say: "Let us leave in London this old dusty document and let us write our own constitution and everything will be in order".
But those who still believe in the rule of law and who think that compliance is part of our tradition and our civilisation, and the best way to avoid trouble in the future, should however be reminded that legally speaking that part of the British North America Act which still comes under the British Parliament will continue applying to Canada as long as it hasn't been officially repealed by the same Parliament. In our system, a law simply doesn't die . ..
And the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) should listen to that-
. .. although it becomes obsolete.
There is no doubt that our constitution exists; there is no doubt and we must never forget that a constitution is the fabric of a country. In their constitution, the citizens of a country give shape to the type of life which seems best suited to their ideals and they develop government institutions best designed to promote its realisation.
Our constitution is old, very old indeed. Its roots go back to another century. It cannot be that bad, since over the years Canadians have been able to get by; but it is clear that it does no longer meet the demands of our modern era: television, jets, automobiles, did not exist when the Fathers of the Confederation wrote the constitution. But something remains beyond doubt: the efforts of the Canadian government, particularly under the thrust and the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau)-has gone beyond the call of duty in an effort to amend and improve our Canadian Constitution including its patriation.
I think that the federal government, more than any other government, has taken every possible care to meet that challenge and its own objectives. It is unfair and I insist on this point, as I would like all the hon. members of the House fully realize it-to claim that the very hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) lacks flexibility on constitutional matters. His government has published a series of papers clearly explaining the powers he intended to retain and the concessions he was prepared to make. We only have to refer to some documents published by the government: the Canadian Charter of Human Rights in January 1968, "Federalism for the Future" in February of the same year and "Federalism and International Relations", "Federalism and International Conferences on Education", in 1968, "The Constitution and the People of Canada" and "The Taxing Powers and the Constitution of Canada" in June 1969. Finally, we had a report entitled "Federal-Provincial Grants and the Spending Powers of Par-

liament". In December 1969, the government published a report entitled "Income Security and Social Services".
We have evidence that the Canadian government did all it could to clear the way and to create the conditions for dialogue and to promote the constitutional process. The federal government certainly cannot be faulted for inflexibility and immobil-ism. On the contrary, I think the major problem lies in the fact that the ten provincial premiers want to eat their soup, their meat and their dessert at the same time instead of going step by step, as we normally do, and having first soup, then meat before finishing the meal with dessert. This means, as far as the constitution is concerned, that we should start first by patriating the Canadian constitution and then we should try to find an amending formula which would be acceptable to all parties concerned. Then, we could negotiate new amendments to the Canadian constitution as far as taxation and responsibilities are concerned. Mr. Speaker, I think it is essential to go step by step and follow the recommendation of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and at least start meeting this goal, I mean the patriation of the constitution.
I cannot think that the new government in Quebec will not agree with the Canadian government to get rid as soon as possible of this last remnant of our colonial past: the Canadian constitution is still in London whereas it should be in Ottawa.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the peroration of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) and his analysis of the non-status of the parliament of Canada, I want simply to reaffirm my faith in the parliament of Canada, in my right to be present in this chamber as the representative of the people who elected me, and my belief that this institution is fundamental to the existence of Canada as a sovereign nation. The motion before us today serves one purpose and one purpose only, and it is this: to bring the issue of constitutional reform out from the secret conclaves of federal-provincial conferences, down from the realm of the Prime Minister's intellectual musings and into the reality of parliamentary debate.
Free democratic countries regard their constitutions, whether they be bodies of law or bodies of conventions or a mixture of these two, as the sure foundation to their well-being. Canada is not different in this regard. We have been building our constitution for almost 110 years. It is a massive, even unwieldy instrument. It creaks and groans as it labours along, it allows for conflict and even misinterpretation-but given the will and the determination, it works.
The question is, do the governments who today are responsible for its implementation have the will and the strength to make it work? Like so many other Canadians, I am beginning to doubt it. Patriation of the constitution is an objective which all Canadians share. A few, I suspect, give it a much higher priority than do the majority. As an unabashed Canadian nationalist, I have long wanted to see the Canadian constitu-
December 3, 1976

tion domiciled in Canada. My leader and former leaders of my party have reiterated that sentiment on many occasions. The question is not whether or not we should have patriation, but how and to what extent it should take priority over the other issues that face the country.
Patriation should come about in such a way as to strengthen the bonds of confederation and confirm our commitment to our duly constituted institutions. It should avoid, at all costs, exacerbating the very real tensions that are increasingly evident in this country. Simple patriation carried out with the concurrence of the federal partner only-a procedure to which the minister referred as a last resort-would be a hollow symbolic gesture which, while it might serve to bolster the Prime Minister's ego, would be a divisive tactic, another needless irritant to the provincial partners. I very much doubt that such a move would have the endorsement of the majority of Canadians who, above all else, want to be reassured that the partnership which we call confederation is still that-a partnership.
Canadian sovereignty on symbolic issues cannot be expressed in a vacuum, devoid of reality. Canada is a federal state and always has been. Most Canadians have a healthy commitment to federalism and recognize the virtues of distributing governmental functions between a central government and governments of the component units of the federation. Indeed, that is what many of the important provisions of the BNA Act set out to do. Over a century of experience in the art of federalism has provided Canadians with workable political structure which is the envy of many countries throughout the world, given our complexities and diversities. Our federalism is itself an achievement, both substantive and symbolic; and it implies a rejection of the extremes of both centralism and decentralism.
To suggest that a document so basic to our federal structure be transferred from Great Britain to Canada without the agreement of the provinces is to ignore the fundamental basis of our political and constitutional system. Not only would this cause real damage to long-established relationships between the provinces and Ottawa but, more important, it would bring about such a transfer without any agreement as to an amending formula by which the document in future could be changed.
Simple patriation, even with the unanimous consent of the federal and provincial governments, while a laudable step in the right direction is still largely symbolic. Without federal-provincial agreement on an amending formula to ensure that what we put in place in Canada is a workable, amendable document and not something that is tied up in a blue or a red ribbon and kept on a shelf for decorative purposes-as would be the case for a document for which there is no amending procedure-we will have achieved an exercise in futility. Imagine the frustration of this chamber and of corresponding provincial legislatures of having the major body of law in Canada incapable of amendment. What a legacy for this
The Constitution
government and this parliament to leave to future generations! It would be nothing but a cop-out on the part of the government of the day.
As recently as in 1972, the Senate-Commons Committee on the Constitution of Canada, jointly chaired and dominated by the Liberal majority in the twenty-eighth parliament, stated:
It would be unwise to proceed with patriation in the absence of agreement on an amending procedure.
Canada is a mature nation. It is no longer an experiment. But if we are to grow in our maturity, symbolic gestures, however momentarily satisfying, are not enough. Maturity is gauged by substantive measures, and substantive measures, above all else, are based on trust. But that basic ingredient of trust, so necessary for sound federalism, has been grievously lacking in recent years as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has pursued the path of confrontation with the provinces. Until there is greater trust and greater mutual respect between the partners in confederation we will go on discussing symbolic gestures rather than the substantive realities which this country has to face.
I, for one, believe that the present federal government, given its past history of dictatorial utterances, unilateral moves and broken promises, is incapable of restoring trust and respect in this country.
Hear, hear!

They appear neither to have the will to accomplish it nor, regretfully, even to see the need to accomplish it. A constitutional debate, whether it concerns patriation, the power to amend, or the redistribution of powers, is a debate to which all Canadians must feel they have the right to contribute.
I made reference earlier to the secrecy of federal and provincial conferences, the number of which has increased dramatically in recent years. If we stop to analyse it, we find that more substantial decisions about the future of this country are now being made at in-camera federal-provincial meetings than in all our combined legislative chambers. That is a trend about which I have serious misgivings. Very shortly we shall be faced with legislation dealing with new fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments-massive fiscal arrangements which could drastically alter the economic bases of confederation.
Face it fast.
Discussions have been going on for months on the singularly important matter. And where? Behind closed doors to which only a select few are privy.
This is wrong.
Oh, oh!
You are the government of the day. Start remembering it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let the lady speak.

One expects continuing negotiation to be carried on with some degree of privacy, but surely on an issue of this magnitude the whole question of the new fiscal arrangements involving some $10 billion, and the fundamental concept of equalization, the matter should be debated in principle in this House prior to the start of negotiations.
Hear, hear!

To do otherwise, as has become the practice, is to erode the influence, the integrity and the raison d'etre of this great national institution-parliament. The continuing erosion of the strength of this national institution lessens its credibility with Canadians, diminishes its meaning and encourages a drift into regionalism and parochialism. The country becomes the poorer for it, as region competes with region and Canadians lose their sense of Canadianism.
I have just returned from Israel. In that country nobody asks whether it is "rentable" to be an Israeli. Most of us forget what a diversity there is among the people of Israel. Its citizens and their fathers have come from all over the world, from many different national and linguistic backgrounds, from western, central, and eastern Europe, from Asia and Africa, from the greatest imaginable differences of economic and social backgrounds-not only the eminent scholars and scientists we have heard about but many thousands of the poor, the illiterate, the peasants of other lands for whom going to Israel from where they had lived was like going forward not one, but several, generations in time.
Some would say that what unifies Israel is that they have lived for almost 30 years in mortal peril of their existence. That is far from being the essence of the story. The essence is that Israel is an idea, and for that idea there have been enormous sacrifices and enormous achievement. I am not referring to the wars they have had to fight; I am thinking of what they have done in spite of war.
Canada, too, is an idea. The idea did not spring from the theory of government. Nobody left us a version of the federalist papers. The idea of Canada has evolved over 110 years. The year 1867 was important. It had to do with our vulnerability to the United States; it had to do with our trade and economic potential; it had to do with the preservation of language rights

and systems of law; it had to do with the failure of previous systems of government; it had to do with some peoples' vision of a "new nationality" across this continent. Yes, 1867 was important. But so were 1870, 1871, 1873, 1905 and 1949-
Hear, hear!

-when the new provinces joined confederation and being a Canadian took on new aspects and new dimensions with added responsibilities, new perspectives. The Fathers of Confederation in 1867 did not have the last word about Canada, nor should the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) think that he has, or is, the last word on the subject. Nor should any prime minister or parliament hold that view.
Our search is not for an ultimate truth, either to find one or to impose one. Our duty is to pass on this country to our successors unified, vital, improved by our efforts with the expectation that further changes will be necessary as Canadian society changes.
The idea of Canada and the destiny of Canada will not be found in political theory or constitutional law. To talk to Canadians about their country exclusively in those terms is almost as sterile as talking about "federalisme rentable". No, Canada has not been the work of constitutional lawyers. The Canada we want to build cannot be defined or expressed or, indeed, realized in terms of distribution of powers, or as a set masterpiece of political theory. The average Canadian does not see it that way. What Canadian, if asked to explain his country or his feeling for his country, does so in terms of the British North America Act?
Canada has been a painstaking work of accommodation and reconciliation from the beginning. I am not referring only to differing points of view about language and culture, but also to the views of the anti-confederates in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and more recently in Newfoundland as dramatic examples, and the many accomplishments in the face of such events which have only been possible because of a spirit of accommodation in this country.
The blackest moments in our history and the most lamentable turning points have come when the spirit of mutual generosity and reconciliation has been set aside and partisan, sectional, or short term interests allowed to prevail. It happened even under the greatest prime ministers; the hanging of Riel under Macdonald, and the virtual abandonment by Lauri-er of federal responsibility for the educational rights of Franco-Manitobans.
However, the most shortsighted view of all is to see Canada today as a power struggle between contending governments in Ottawa and the provinces. Governments and their bureaucracies will always contend; it is in their nature to do so. That is not the problem of confederation today. The problem is that this country is becoming increasingly fragmented. But regionalism as a popular sentiment ceases to be a source of vitality for the country and becomes a menace when it is directed against something, and especially against national institutions
December 3, 1976

and national leadership. That happens when people become convinced that those institutions and that leadership do not represent what they are and what they mean to Canada. The result of that insensitivity is called alienation, and there is too much of it everywhere in Canada today.
It is said that the Prime Minister came into federal politics to fight Quebec nationalism. That may be his purpose, but it will not serve as a national purpose. Most Canadians would like to think their country has some higher and more positive purpose after 110 years. Suggesting that because the Quebec government proposes to have a referendum the federal government will have one in the rest of the country shows the paucity of this government's proposals.
Absolute bloody nonsense; a national referendum is the stupidest thing you could be talking about.
Who is speaking here?

The attitudes and actions of this government have not been a force for unity but rather a cause of divisiveness and factionalism. The Prime Minister talks about tribalism. Nothing encourages a retreat to factionalism and regionalism everywhere in Canada more than the spectre of a national government which manifestly does not know about and cares little about the legitimate problems which concern people in different parts of the country in their daily working lives.
Hear, hear!

What is needed is a unifying force. Parliament could still be that unifying force, but the government would first have to restore its integrity and credibility with this institution, the one institution that all Canadians hold in common.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to open by extending my congratulations to the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) and his colleagues for bringing forward in this House the subject we are discussing today. It is in striking contrast to the general tendency of the government of this country, which is to think that you could discuss the constitution, the fundamental law of Canada, anywhere except in parliament.
Right on.

I hope that that will change and that we in parliament will be fully consulted about the things which are
The Constitution
fundamental to the future of our country. Having said that, I also must say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member for Shefford that we totally reject the motion he has brought forward today.

Mr. Speaker, since I am sure the House will give the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) additional time if he needs it, I would like to ask him a very brief question. Why is it that when there have been opposition days the hon. member's party did not use any of them for this important issue? If the government is to be blamed-and I am not too sure the hon. member is not correct-why is it that the hon. member did not raise this issue at the first opportunity, as the Social Credit Party of Canada has done, so that there could be a debate on this subject?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: He wasn't here.

I have no trouble answering that question. We in this party have extremely good intelligence in terms of what is going on, and we knew the hon. member for Shefford was going to introduce this subject.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You weren't even here.

In addition to that, we had a very important subject to bring before the House. It was a subject dealing with the mismanagement of important affairs in this country. We brought that forward, and we are certainly very happy that the hon. member for Shefford has given us a chance to speak on this subject, which we think to be of great importance.
Please speak about the new constitution.

I think I would speak a little better if I were not told exactly what I am supposed to say.
I think it is conventional wisdom generally nowadays amongst many people, including parliamentarians, the press and even some learned people, to speak as if the constitution is unimportant and that the subject matter is fit only for discussion amongst learned constitutional lawyers. I can assure the House that it is a good subject for constitutional lawyers, but it is also a matter which affects everybody.
I want to quote from a document which I will be quoting from again. It is the final report on the Constitution of Canada of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons of which the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) was one of the joint chairmen. It includes some 103 recommendations, some sage observations, and some suggestions which are perhaps not feasible. I do not know; I am not putting it forward as the last word of wisdom. All I am saying is that it is a rather remarkable thing that this report was produced in 1972, with many constructive proposals, and has practically never been discussed in this House. I think the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and myself have mentioned it once in a blue moon, but it has really not

December 3, 1976
The Constitution
been adequately discussed in this House. I hope recent events will cause it to be looked at seriously once more.
In chapter 3 the report reads:
The purpose of a constitution is to distribute the powers of government according to the wishes of a particular national community-
May I stop there and say that that, of course, is an important function. You cannot operate a system in a vast area like Canada, with different and disparate regions, without having some instrument that distributes powers. That is what our constitution does and must do if we are to have a constitution.
It goes on:
-and to enunciate its fundamental values and common goals. A constitution ought thus to be both an inspiration and a mirror for its community. Of these two ends its inspirational role is the more important. A community that is unable to justify its existence to itself will eventually find that it cannot survive by structure alone.
I should like to say that our present constitution is grossly inadequate in this respect. The British North America Act may have been wisely thought of and conceived by our forefathers, but its expression is in no way suited to the present time. We urgently need a new statement of principle and purpose which would include, for example, our devotion to the partnership of the two founding peoples or nations of this country. We need a constitution to state clearly our acceptance of basic, fundamental human rights such as could be elaborated in a constitutional bill of rights rather than the partial bill of rights we have at the present time. We need to refer to purposes, removing regional disparities, giving a fair deal to our native population, and we need a statement, in a preamble or prospectus, of the sort of things that the constitution should include and which should be put forward as an aim, as an objective of the activities of the people of Canada.
We urgently need that, and in the strictures given by the hon. member for Shefford with reference to the British North America Act at least he was totally accurate in the statement that it is obsolete and that it no longer fitted the facts, and that some new constitution was required. He was just in saying the reason it was like that was because it was conceived in a time of colonialism, conceived in a colonial era, conceived in circumstances that are no longer with us, and it therefore has become an anachronism that requires to be changed. But the resolution reads:
That this House condemns the central government for threatening the provinces with a unilaterally imposed patriation of a constitution which is obsolete and no longer responds to the aspirations of Canadians, rather than, as it should, leaving to the provinces the task of drafting a new constitution.
It is clear from this motion that he sees no participation whatever by representatives of this parliament; that the provinces alone are to get together in some sort of constituent assembly-a difficult thing to arrange-and out of that a constitution would emerge.
I think this parliament has an obligation of leadership in bringing about developments and changes that are required in
(Mr. Brcwin.]
our constitution. I reject the theory that we should be totally eliminated from the picture.
As for the hon. member's proposition that because of some of the imperfections and now anachronistic provisions of the BN A Act-which, of course, was not the only act-that somehow or other we have not even got a constitution, I reject that totally. He said it was not ratified by the people. Mr. Speaker, we have had millions of people vote in this country from every part of the country, people sit in this House from every part of Canada; there are federal-provincial conferences, and representatives of this government are throughout the world. He cannot turn back the pages of history. His essay was well done and interesting but it had no bearing on the realities of the facts.
Canada is Canada; this parliament is here; it is a fact of history. We do not propose to abdicate our function simply because of some essay about the imperfections in the way it was founded. If there are, and I believe there are, some remaining traces of colonialism which are in no way essential to us, then we have to get rid of them. That brings me to the question of patriation.
I doubt if any member of this House thinks that patriation is not desirable. The right to amend the constitution of Canada clearly at the present time rests with the imperial parliament. They do not want that responsibility, and it is a most obvious anachronism that it should exist. The reason it exists is that we have been unable to agree to the amending formula which must go with repatriation. I think it was the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) who said, and I am paraphrasing her, that it would be absolutely ridiculous to think we could suddenly bring some document over from England, take it from Westminster and put it here or somewhere else in Canada, and say that now we have the piece of paper and it is repatriated, unless we make it a living thing. The living thing would fill in the serious gap in the present situation, and that is that there is no method of amending, no method except the implied one, of going back to ask the imperial parliament all over again to assume responsibility for the future affairs of Canada. That would be absolutely silly.
If the proposal is to repatriate the constitution without an amending formula, then I say it would be going through a parade of words which would satisfy nobody's national ego and would be a foolish and futile gesture.
We do not have to worry too much about an amending formula. In my judgment a very sensible compromise was arrived at-not fully ratified, it is true-at the Victoria conference. It came between the two extremes: those who said that the federal parliament should unilaterally amend the constitution of Canada, which I think would be quite wrong and quite impossible, and the other extreme which gave absolute powers of a straitjacket-which put the constitution in a straitjacket requiring unanimity of every province. We went through that in the last decade.
We had the Fulton formula, the Favreau formula, then the Fulton-Favreau formula. The basic weakness of those formulas was that they proposed unanimity before any change could be

made. The Victoria formula provides for a measure of consensus. In my view it provides justly for the two major provinces to give consent before changes are made.
One of our members has suddenly sprouted out as a constitutional expert, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson). You do not understand that.

I do not think he understands it either. Frankly, the Victoria formula is a perfectly reasonable formula, consensus but not veto. I do not know why it cannot be adopted. It could be adopted as a formula both for repatriating the constitution and creating a form of amendment and it could be the start of a totally new approach.
I think with some confidence that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is perfectly correct in saying that under our present legal rules, leaving out conventions for the moment, a unilateral request from this parliament would be enough to persuade the British government to act and make the amendment being sought. It would be extremely foolish at this time of great sensitivity, as far as the future of Canada is concerned, for the Prime Minister to seek to impose this. I am glad to know that he has yielded gracefully-although I did not observe the grace-to the suggestion made by the new Prime Minister of Quebec that this particular subject not be debated at the immediately forthcoming conference. This debate on the constitution enables me to say one or two things that may not be strictly relevant to the resolution. I want to announce, as others have, including the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, my firm belief in the future of a federal Canada, of a united Canada. We do not wish to see this country broken up. There are many reasons for that. It will be our function as members of parliament in the next few

years to get out and see that the people of Canada understand some of the reasons.
In my judgment one of the basic reasons is that to break up the federal nature of Canada would greatly weaken us in our international role. We have an important contribution to make in the world as a whole. I have been told that by people who were not just trying to flatter me as a Canadian, but people who have thought about it. They believe there is a great deal that Canada can do.
One of the sources of great strength of Canada in the international world is that we are bilingual by and large, and that we represent two different founding races. We are, of course, enriched by cultures from other parts of the world. However, this fact of bilingualism and biculturalism adds tremendous strength to the international image of Canada.
I want to explain to our constituents and others throughout the country our contribution to dealing with some of the main forces that indirectly, intentionally or otherwise, threaten the independence of our country. Let us never forget that we are the neighbour of an immense super power with tremendously attractive politics. Neither French speaking nor English speaking Canada is desirous of being weakened vis-a-vis our neighbour. We are friendly with our neighbour.

In all this hubbub of cacophonous reactions from all quarters, we may have forgotten the only reaction which really counted, that of the Quebec people. What did happen in la Belle Province on November 15? Whether you were a white-collar worker, a blue-collar worker, a wage-earner, a farmer, an unemployed person or someone on social welfare, you all felt this puff of fresh and vitalizing air over the province of Quebec. First of all, it was a sound lesson taught to a spineless and unscrupulous government which was sleeping on his laurels after its tremendous victory in 1973. It also proved that the Prime Minister of this country was right last spring when he went to Quebec City to box the ears of his old friend "Ti-Pit" while partaking of a copious meal with this "hot dog eater", as he called him.
Mr. Speaker, I am telling you, the people of Quebec had the feeling that the sweet breeze of liberty and independence was following in the wake of this terrible sweeping storm. Many things have occurred which induce the people of Quebec to accelerate from now on the pace of history. One of those things is worth mentioning and it is the fantastic contribution made by the present Prime Minister, the hon. member for Mount Royal.
Indeed, since that famous 1967 conference, where the then minister of justice confronted his federalist thesis with that of the then Quebec Premier, the lamented Daniel Johnson, who waved the flag of equality or independence, the chips are down. Obstinately, paradoxically and at times arrogantly, the leader of the federal Liberal Party did everything in his power to force all Canadians, and in particular Quebecers, to become aware of their own identity.
The more he attempted to convince them of the value of bilingualism, the more every one of the Canadian ethnic group realized that they wanted to preserve their own language. The more we tried to make regional disparities disappear, the more each area wanted to jealously protect its prerogatives. The more attempts were made to set up a centralizing federalism and a central government, the more the provinces took care to safeguard their rights and privileges. As a good dyed in wool Quebecer, I must congratulate the Prime Minister for having been instrumental in that essential and salutary crisis.
However, he carries on his exceptional work doggedly, without flinching. As early as election night on November 15, his reaction seen by millions of televiewers made a sensation. He easily convinced a great number of citizens who had not voted for the PQ that it was essential to support the new government in order to achieve independence. His spontaneous statements leave no doubt; he shouts: "Long live a united Canada" so as to ascertain "Long live a free Quebec." I fully agree with him.
One day, history will recognize the efficiency of his action. We must realize where the true problem lies. It is not a matter of pitting the supporters of federalism against the supporters of independence; it is rather a question of recognizing that like the other Canadians, the people in Quebec will find their identity one day. Recently a good friend of mine who is now lawyer in Sherbrooke, Mr. Georges Labrecque, wrote a paper on the subject. This article was published in the newspapers Le

Devoir and La Tribune. I received a photostat of the original from which I shall quote extensively with your permission:
It is not possible to win a Quebecer to endorse independance. He himself feels this need or not. Endorsing this idea is a phenomenon of perception rather than an act of understanding. It is a mistake to believe that merely through logical arguments or incentives, someone will endorse independence. Such endorsement results from an awareness. The latter comes from accumulated actions which lead a person to seek his identity. This group identification evolves by means of comparisons with other entities. As long as our people called themselves "Cana-diens" and called the others "English", the identity problem did not arise but once they realized that they were not or were no longer "Canadiens", the search was on. It is a long but inevitable process. The group is redefining itself. Once the definition is complete, a new nation is born. Territory delineation follows the collective feeling of belonging. A true nation lives first in the heart of its inhabitants.
The more television, radio and publicity make the other entity known, the more acute becomes the awareness. The more the definition and identification process of a Quebecer is stepped up, the more the gap between him and the "Canadien" widens. The campaign of propaganda conducted by the federal government to strengthen national unity proves to be the ideal process leading to independence.
For generations, Quebecers did not make any comparisons. They were themselves and they identified themselves with Canada because they were Canada. They are now discovering another Canada.
The traditional nationalism met the aspirations of the times. To all intents and purposes, it did not destroy the established patterns. Henri Bourassa's nationalism was the weapon of the times, if nothing but a defensive weapon. Besides, it was well suited to the people's will, since the great majority still identified with the word "Canada".
In Papineau's time, identification through comparison was not necessary. National identification was a matter of fact. At that time, the problem was not one of national identification, but of liberation. Liberation was not the mental phenomenon it is today, it was a confrontation with power. The conquerers' bondage was recent and the fear of external domination remained.
Young people today identify themselves naturally. Identification as a Canadian is too complicated for it does not square with reality. The identification with Quebec is theirs, the problem is simple, they look at the patterns of others and reject them. By discarding established principles, by defining themselves they identify with the Quebec community. Whether they are politically oriented or not, they are Quebecers. The teachers cannot do anything about it; the young people reject offhand the definition of "Canadien" that their parents are trying to foist on them.
During World War I, Quebecers became collectively aware-they identified themselves. The war phenomenon was tremendous, the two solitudes found themselves facing a common problem, but they found themselves face to face: the two nations had an entirely different position on war. The issue was important and the positions were poles apart. During World War II, the phenomenon occurred again: communications improved between the groups and the identification went further on. A party-the Bloc populaire-was born. Its success in terms of popular vote was amazing. The communication of national identification was accidental and temporary, so the project aborted.
Around the sixties, bombs exploded. Some became aware of a reality that they wanted to bring to the fore. It is true indeed, there are two peoples in Canada; perhaps two nations, nobody knows. Ignorance used to prevail. The true Canada is born. There are French-Canadians and English-Canadians here. The masks are removed, people are wondering. There are two of us in the same house. Are we married? Do we have a contract? English-Canadians would watch us coming out of our box and ask: What does Quebec want?
For us, it was difficult to bear. Others had taken our name and even questioned our right to be here. They were awe-struck as they watched us get out of our box. The French-Canadians realized that they had not even been noticed-our people then got down on the street and started to demonstrate. Saint-John the Baptist Day proved not enough; the time of peaceful marches was over, people got tough and started smashing things around.
But, Ottawa had known the situation for along time. Now they knew that the people knew, and that desperate ills call for desperate remedies. Pearson,

Mr. Speaker, this attempt at merging two different groups has indeed failed because, whether we want it or not, there is now a Canadian issue. It is the duty of this House to stay calm cool-headed and forward-looking. Now the provinces must have priority. They alone can indicate, through a referendum if necessary, which powers they wish to keep under their own jurisdictions and which ones they are willing to entrust to a central administration. However, we can already see that the national currency would remain under the control of the government of the Canadian common market, while credit would be under the exclusive control of provinces. Each province would use its actual credit by calling upon the financial services of the Bank of Canada Branch. For instance, Quebec and Ontario would be responsible for credit distribution just like Hydro-Quebec and Ontario Hydro are responsible for the distribution of electricity. The federal government could not en danger the financial credit of each province, and neither would any province be able to endanger that of another province.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, in closing I would like to quote a passage from my publicity pamphlet which was distributed during our convention on November 6 and 7 last. It is entitled: "A New Canada", and I quote:
In this vast country of Canada, irresponsible governments have succeeded in creating a lack of understanding, resentment and even hate! People do not even know each other from one region to another, but they still cordially detest one another. This causes disastrous stands to be taken and doubtful policies to be developed.
We are adults, but we still fight like children to know who is responsible for whom and for what. We are unable to determine clearly provincial and federal jurisdictions. Yet, some people are interested in maintaining this ambiguous situation which often verges on ridicule!
Quebec might vote for independence very shortly and the government proposes to patriate the constitution! They want to impose another language against the rights and privileges that should be granted to any human being.
And yet there is a solution to this problem. Each Canadian entity should be allowed to choose its own rights, privileges and jurisdictions. Not only Quebec but also Ontario, the Maritime provinces, the Prairies and British Columbia would be new states; they would determine their own jurisdictions and those they would share jointly within a true confederation which would bring about a new and diversified but really harmonious Canada.
We should no longer advocate unconditionally that out-ofdate system which, as was clearly proved by my colleague from Shefford has never been anything more than John A. Macdonald's obsession.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau). I would have liked to try to answer in French if my colleague from Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, had not already done so in very eloquent French. In the circumstances, I prefer to speak in English.
[Mr. Matte.)
The hon. member for Shefford treated us to a very interesting speech, but I must admit that for a long time I was quite lost in discovering what was its possible point. It was a very interesting historical account, a combination of one part fantasy with another part of unwarranted inference from historical facts, aided by a great deal of purple prose descriptive of the events of the 19th century in language that was worthy of that century, and supported from time to time by actual quotations from historical documents.
This melange was such that it was only when he was well along in his speech that it was possible to ascertain the point of it all. The point, as I understand it, is that Sir John A. Macdonald betrayed the people of this country in order to gain a wife and an honour from the Queen. The alternate theory behind the historical exposition, if I might call it that, of the hon. member for Shefford was that a federal system can only be a federal system if it corresponds to the very narrow definition which the hon. member would wish a federal state to have. It was in the context of this Procrustean bed that he analyzed all of the constitutional history and law.
I think we should look only briefly, because I have a number of different points I want to touch on, at the actual historical facts at the time. It may be that people who live in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick could make some kind of claim that their governments did not approve the Quebec resolutions on which the act of 1867 was based, but no such claim is possible for those who live in the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec.
In the combined province of Ontario and Quebec a resolution was introduced in the parliament of 1865. That resolution, which was for the adoption of the Quebec resolutions of the previous year, was supported by that assembly by a vote of 91 to 33. I think it worth noting that, although there were not the divisions of Ontario and Quebec existing at that time in a legal sense, the majority of French members of the assembly also supported this resolution, the vote of the French members being 27 in favour and 22 opposed. However you look at this, Mr. Speaker, whether you look at it as a vote of that assembly as a whole or as a vote of the English and French members, there is no doubt that both groups as well as the whole assembly favoured the Quebec resolutions.
I will not deal with the situation in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I think most historians and political scientists are satisfied that the legislatures of those provinces through appointed delegations did eventually accept confederation. We are concerned here, as a result of the motion presented by the hon. member for Shefford, about the attitude of the people in Ontario and Quebec.
He attempted to draw a sharp distinction between the Quebec resolutions of 1864 and the actual act of 1867, the British North America Act. There were a few verbal differences. It is true that the British authorities did not want us to have the title for the country that we wanted. I believe that

originally the Fathers of Confederation wanted the name the United Kingdom of Canada, and I suspect most Canadians today are rather happy that that suggestion did not carry and that the word "kingdom," which was conceived by the British as being unacceptable to the Americans, was eventually cast aside in favour of "dominion", a word which itself is not considered by everyone to be a full description of our status at the present time.
There were some other verbal changes, mostly as a matter of putting the resolutions into legal form. The chief objection the British raised at that time to the Quebec resolutions was in respect of the Senate. They wanted a provision for the appointment of additional senators in the case of deadlock in the Senate, and indeed that was adopted as part of the final bill.
These are the changes, and the only changes, that were made between the act of 1867 and the Quebec resolutions of 1864. There is no substantial difference. Any difference in verbiage does not indicate a difference between a conception of the union which was held by the people in Ontario and Quebec on the one hand and by the British government on the other. It was common coin at that time that we were dealing with colonies which in a sense were self-governing, but nevertheless colonies which in many respects, especially in defence and foreign affairs, were subject to Great Britain.
I would be the last to say, since I was involved in a report which criticized very strongly this document, the act of 1867, that the British North America Act as it stands is satisfactory. I think it is precisely because it was conceived in this colonial atmosphere, and because of other changes in the world which have taken place in the course of time, that that Act is no longer satisfactory as it is. I have said so in writing many times. But this is not to say that it was not what the people wanted. It was what the Fathers of Confederation wanted, even though it may not be what we want. I do not think we do our cause any useful service today, whether it be the cause of the Social Credit party or the cause of any other party, in looking at historical facts in a way other than that which is strictly factual.
To come back to the Procrustean bed I have mentioned, to which the hon. member would confine federalism, he quoted some definitions of federalism. There are hundreds of experts in this area, of whom he quoted two. One could look at the classic analysis of people like K. C. Wheare and others. Wheare regarded Canada as a quasi-federalism. Other people have classified it in different ways.
In a very interesting paper of few years ago Professor Mallory of McGill spoke about five faces of federalism in Canada, and suggested that Canada itself had passed through all those stages of federalism. In other words federalism is not a single thing. It is a living reality. There is no way in which we can adopt some abstract definition of federalism which is taken by someone from observing the American constitution, probably before 1867, and say that if it is not like this it is not federalism.
One of the definitions of federalism which is given, and which I think is a general one which is reasonably descriptive,
The Constitution
is by W. H. Riker from the book "Federalism: Origin, Operation, Significance" published in 1964. I quote this because it is an American authority and can be presumed to have no axe to grind in respect of any debate within Canada. Riker defines federalism as a constitution which provides for two levels of government, each of which has some guarantee, even though merely a statement in the constitution, of its contained autonomy within its sphere. In other words there are two kinds of governments, each having a certain degree of authority but no particular kind of origin, no particular kind of amending formula, no particular kind of mechanism for bringing it into operation initially. Those things are determined by historical fact and not by the definitions of political scientists. The fact that the hon. member has been able to find two from the multitude of people who have given useful quotations proves nothing about the significance of federalism in Canada.
He also quoted the Statute of Westminster and suggested that our government here has been, if I can find here his whimsical phrase, in a state of anarchy since December 11, 1931. The Statute of Westminster was basically a document of liberation for the self-governing dominions. It recognized what had been evolving and happening up to that time, but because of the fact that Canadians could not agree on how to amend their constitution then, and as a matter of fact we still haven't as we know, we were exempt from some provisions of that legislation. Section 7 of the Statute of Westminster, which my friend opposite quoted several times, says: "Nothing in this act shall be deemed to apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Act" and so on.
In other words it was not affecting what was already existing. It was not destroying it. It was leaving it untouched. It was saying that with the agreement of Canadians we are not going to do anything about this. It goes on in subsection 3 to provide that the already accepted division of powers between parliament and the legislatures in Canada should remain intact in the future as in the past without being altered by this document, the Statute of Westminster.
I think then we come to the essence of the resolution which has been presented by members of the Social Credit Party here today, that it should be the provinces which should draft a new constitution. As I said, I agree with them that we would be better off with a new constitution, but I am far from agreeing with them that this is a matter which belongs only to the provinces. We live in a country with two levels of government, and obviously the federal government has at least as great a role to play in drafting a new constitution as do the provinces. Our country has been proceeding on that basis for 100 years. He who would suggest that we have been living in illegality for 40 years or 60 years or 100 years is living in an unreal world.
I want to say a few words about the amending formula itself because this is a matter of some interest today. I listened to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) earlier talking about the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution which stated that we did not believe we should

patriate the constitution to Canada without an amending formula. I am still very much of that mind. I think that it would be sheer folly for us to attempt patriation of the constitution without having some agreement as to what we could do with it once it arrived back. This would be putting us in a situation of unparalleled rigidity in a modern state, a situation in which we would probably not be able to amend the constitution at all or, if we did, it would be because of some emergency which had arisen which was so extraordinary that it forced the hand of all of us. But that is a poor way to draft a constitution. A constitution should be the product of mature reflection, and should reflect all realities of the country, not just those which may be perceived as being most pressing during a sudden emergency.
I am very pleased that the government has kept its options open on this matter and that no decision has been made that anything of this kind will happen. Indeed it is hard to imagine that the government would proceed to force its will on the provinces in this respect for the sake of patriation without a formula. I would be quite happy to support the government of Canada in effectively using its unilateral power to impose an amending formula-if we were to have an amending formula along with patriation-provided the amending formula were something as reasonable as the Victoria charter which provides for a reasonable voice for all parts of the country: a majority of six provinces plus the federal government with two central provinces, two from the east and two from the west concurring in a proposed amendment. If it came to that, I think that might well be a proposal which would be worth enacting. It would be worth while for this parliament to use its power by way of a resolution to ask the British parliament-with or without the consent of the provinces if it cannot be obtained- to proceed to a formula of that kind. But to use the unilateral power-which we really possess only once under this act- merely with respect to patriation, because once we patriate the constitution we would no longer have the ability to go to the British parliament, would be to plunge ourselves into a constitutional pit from which I can see no exit. As I say, our government wisely has not committed itself to that course of action.
It would be unrealistic to talk of any of these subjects today without recognizing the fact that the whole situation has changed as a result of the installation of the Partie Quebecois government in the province of Quebec. Up to now I have been talking about these questions, and especially the amending formula, as if the situation were the same, but it is not the same and we have to take this new reality into account.
Another hon. member suggested it is worth looking back for examples, especially to the report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution. That report recommended both more decentralization and more centralization, more decentralization with respect to cultural and social affairs, and more centralization with respect to economic affairs. I believe, the report in balance came down on the side of more decentralization, if one can work out such a balance. I think it is worth while looking back to this report because it is based on

principle. It does not attempt, on the basis of a momentary crisis, to decide what should happen, but rather it proceeds on a longer term basis.
I have to take issue with the leader of the NDP who, in his television address last week, said, after correctly quoting what the committee recommended, that instead of encouraging the implementation of such proposals-that is proposals of the constitution committee-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has totally ignored this all-party report. These are not the facts.
I do not have time to go into all the ways in which the government has implemented that report in the last 4'/2 years since its presentation, but let me give a brief recital of the respects in which government policy has been formulated along the lines recommended by that committee. I will list them briefly. They are: official bilingualism in the constitution; multiculturalism; tri-level conferences between the provinces and municipalities; a broader equalization formula with respect to bringing the municipal level of government into account in equalization; sharing of the family allowances mechanism; broadcasting-we recommended greater provincial powers with respect to educational broadcasting; appointment of senators from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories; an entirely new structure of appointing senators; paramount power with respect to foreign ownership and with respect to the problem of national unity, a power which the federal government has been assuming more and more; the whole movement toward decentralization, which is perhaps the most prominent aspect of implementation within the federal government itself; and reconfirmation in that report of positions which the federal government was taking before that time on such matters as openness with respect to Senate appointments and appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada and with respect to limitations on the spending power.
All of these are ways in which the report is continuing to be implemented by the federal government. I think this indicates that we have a good deal of leadership provided by the federal government, even with respect to decentralization, but as the Prime Minister pointed out last week-

speechtext: Order, please. I thought the hon. member was rising to ask a question, and if so I want to have the consent of the hon. member for Windsor-Walker-ville (Mr. MacGuigan).

I apologize, Mr. Speaker, but there has to be a bit of a preamble to my question. I am sure the issue the hon. member is raising is of great importance to the country. I am astounded, and I do not say this is an argumentative sense. It seems to me that the issue the Prime Minister, my leader, and other leaders in the country are talking about is that this country is an indivisible one. It has also been said that if we accept that, how can we take the position that there should be endorsed by the Parliament of Canada a national referendum on something which is not of itself legitimate? I realize that the hon. member is sincerely concerned about this issue. So am I and so are other hon. members of the House.
I also have in mind the hon. member's considerable expertise in the law, for which I have great respect, but how, if constitutionally and legally this country is indivisible, can we take a course which offers a policy which puts the whole divisibility of this country into issue with the endorsement of the Parliament of Canada of a national referendum? We just cannot logically have both, and it is a very dangerous notion to put forward. I ask the hon. member to respond to that because I had hoped that the Prime Minister put forward that statement only in a passing and casual way. It concerns me a great deal and it concerns other hon. members when the hon. member, with his distinguished legal background, comes in to the House this afternoon and endorses this in a more significant way than, I hope, the Prime Minister did.

Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member opposite well enough to know that he is asking his question in good faith, and I will respond in the same way. I am making this statement only for myself. I am not making it for my
The Constitution
party, my leader or anyone else. It is what I believe. I believe this because I do not see this as being a matter of law.
Legally speaking, of course, Quebec cannot secede, and this country must continue, but the life of a country is not just the law. It is also made up of social events, history, and what is happening now, and we are confronted by a situation in which what is in question is precisely the will of the people to continue the legal arrangement.
I do not agree with the attitude of Rene Levesque that this issue will be decided in Quebec alone. I think this issue should be decided by the whole of Canada, and if the rest of Canada can assure Quebec that we want Quebec to continue with us, I think this will have a big impact on the future of that province.
In conclusion, may I say that I think our country is worth preserving. We have a different kind of democracy and a different kind of federalism from others. Our federalism is different from that of other countries of the world. We have a different notion of freedom. It is more in terms of variety than that of our neighbour to the south, which is more in terms of uniformity. We have a contribution to make to the world because we have a large number of French citizens who have forced us to accept diversity, and it is this fact of diversity upon which our national life is based. For this reason I do not know whether Canada could continue without Quebec, but it certainly could not continue as the same kind of country it is now, and I for one would like to urge that we continue to manifest a common will to live together, not just on legalities but in brotherhood and friendship.

Mr. Speaker, some may wonder at the credentials a person such as myself might have to participate in an important debate on the future of our country, and more specifically, with respect to the constitution. I suppose if one's bona fide would have to be produced, the best one I could produce is the one which might be shared by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) in that my antecedents relate to Charlottetown. Growing up in that particular city, one could not help realizing the importance of the conference which took place there more than a century ago which contributed to the essential founding of this nation. I am going to say something a bit later on about that because I think it is essential to the kind of debate we are having this afternoon.
I too am delighted that the opportunity has been presented by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) for us to participate in this debate, although I regret very much the form in which the motion has been put. I find great difficulty understanding, let alone accepting, the position he and his colleagues have put forward. We have to be realistic, as mentioned by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). The former premier of Saskatchewan, the late Ross Thatcher, said a few years ago that if he was to consider 100 priority issues in Saskatchewan at that time, the question of the future of the constitution would have to rank 101. Certainly there are other people in the country who regard the occasional discussion of this issue as not being the most relevant issue with which we are faced, and undergoing

December 3, 1976
The Constitution
the economic and social stresses we are today, one could not sell that particular position short.
In addition, as has already been pointed out, our constitution residing, as it does, in another country makes it somewhat unique. I think at one point the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was quoted as saying that we were the only modern or major country in the world which does not have its own constitution domiciled in its own country. However, the fact may be that the variety of constitutional arrangements which exist in the world today are just about as numerous as the number of nations. Great Britain, where our constitution resides, has functioned relatively successfully for many centuries without a specific constitution, and our neighbours immediately to the south have had a constitution to which they have had almost continuous resort. One might almost think that they had developed constitutionitis.
One has to ask in the first instance about the very nature of the revival of the question at this time. Since the conclusion of the Victoria conference in 1971 it has been abundantly clear that the question of the constitution has not been a lively topic. Certainly in answer to the occasional questions which have been put to the Prime Minister in the House over the past five years he has indicated that there was no real possibility of exploring the constitutional issue any further at the present time.
However, in the early part of this year, I think about the month of March, we began to hear a number of comments from the Prime Minister, and there were initiatives through correspondence with provincial premiers to the effect that suddenly some action would have to be taken. Indeed, the matter had suddenly become such an important one for the Prime Minister that he took a position which he hitherto regarded, I believe, as not only unacceptable but also unworkable, that of unilaterally asking for patriation of the constitution without any effective consensus among the 10 provincial governments. Of course the Prime Minister has made a number of arguments since in support of the fact that it is no longer acceptable to a large number of Canadians that the Canadian constitution not reside in our own country but in another country.
I am not sure in what way he has distilled this wisdom of a sudden shift in the attitude of the Canadian public, but he was able to announce that as a basic fact. In addition, he suggested that increasingly we are being faced with problems which could only be resolved by having the constitution on our own home soil.
When this debate was begun this year, there was an editorial which, more than any other editorial, suggested why the action of the Prime Minister was not only precipitous but fundamentally dangerous. An editorial in the Globe and Mail of March 24, 1976, headed "1867 And All That", read:
Canada is a country of tensions, some of them good, some of them bad, but tensions, nevertheless. Not surprisingly, the dominant characteristic of Canadian politics has been its preoccupation with reconciling those tensions. That is why
[Mr. MacDonald (Egmont).l
the style of Canadian politics has by and large concentrated on the art of compromise, the deliberate dialogue, the negotiated settlement.
I only wish that the Prime Minister had had an opportunity to read those words before he engaged in this round of what is increasingly seen as a rather foolish exercise on his part because it has done little except increase rigidities on the part of provincial governments and, if it is possible, create a situation of even greater mistrust with respect to the objectives, aims, and purposes of the central government. I say this because one surely has to ask why the Prime Minister has asked now for unilateral patriation of the constitution or would move to do this if no consensus could be achieved.
In the same editorial there appears a comment which I think gives an indication of some of the changes inherent in the proposal the Prime Minister put forward. It reads as follows:
Unilateral patriation is said to be possible, because the British parliament would act on the request of the Governor General to transfer the BN A Act to Canada and would not concern itself with whether the provinces agreed. If that is indeed the case, there would be nothing to prevent the federal government from requesting a transfer that would enlarge its rights at the cost of the provinces.
That comment puts a finger on one of the essential problems that would be in this proposal if, as the Prime Minister has argued, it is possible to take this action and wise to take this action. It is not just a question of whether it would be legally acceptable for the federal parliament to legislate the BNA Act back to Canada but whether, on the basis of that precedent, it would then have the opportunity to make unilateral amendments without any kind of consensus or consultation with the provinces. I find it a shocking lack of recognition on the part of the Prime Minister, who is apparently schooled in questions on the constitution, that he can ignore that essential problem. The fact is, of course, that he did not ignore the problem because during debate in the month of April he said that the Parliament of Canada now has the legal right and in fact has exercised that right historically, to act unilaterally in amending the constitution.
The Prime Minister was correct in one sense. As I understand it, a number of amendments to the constitution were achieved unilaterally before the early part of this century, but I would ask the Prime Minister to indicate whether there has been any amendment of the constitution since 1907 without the consent of the provinces involved? Of course there has not. What the Prime Minister is trying to do through his sleight of hand is create a new precedent, or return to a precedent that is no longer acceptable in the practices of this country, and that is to operate by unilateral fiat.
I think the Prime Minister has been understood not only by provincial governments but by the people generally to say that the nature of confederation being what it is and should be, we cannot have one element of the responsible structure of this country acting in this kind of unilateral and irresponsible way. In addition, it is not just a possibility of future unilateral amendments to the constitution which jeopardizes the present situation: there is the even more serious situation which faces us with respect to our own national well-being. The Prime Minister has stressed that what he is hoping to achieve in the
December 3, 1976

first place is simply to patriate the constitution and then at a later date, when there can be some reasonable discussion, the ten provincial governments will arrive at an acceptable amending formula.
If the Prime Minister has some special information about how long it would take to achieve an amending formula, I hope he will share it with the Canadian people. In the half dozen conferences held over the past 50 years on the question of achieving an amending formula, in spite of the tremendous effort of constitutional lawyers and provincial and federal leaders, we have not yet arrived at the golden moment when we have agreed upon a constitutional amending formula.
What the Prime Minister is offering is to patriate the constitution now, and sometime in the future- 10, 15, 25, 50, who knows how many years away-maybe then have an acceptable amending formula. What he is offering is in effect a constitution domiciled in Canada that would be as dead as the dodo. I doubt if there are too many people in this country who would willingly accept that. I believe it to be in the best interests of this country, as I am sure does every other member of the House, that we have our own constitution domiciled in this country.
Hear, hear!

However, if there is one thing that is worse than the present situation of having a constitution in another country, in the final analysis controlled by another parliament, it is that we would have a constitution in our own country that we would not control at all.
Hear, hear!

At least in the present situation, cumbersome as it may be, 22 times since confederation we have been able to amend the constitution-by long distance if you like. Even a constitution which can be amended by long distance is better than a constitution which cannot be touched.
I find it incredible that the Prime Minister should attempt to face Canadians or provincial premiers with that kind of proposition. I presume in the nature of the events that have happened since, that the whole question of some unilateral patriation of the constitution on the terms suggested and defended by the Prime Minister, is now seen to be an incredible proposition and an offence to our social system.
I want to return to some of the essential elements considering the constitution itself. In the beginning I said there are a great variety of constitutions in the world today and, as has been suggested by previous speakers, ours is unique. It has problems associated with it and, as I indicated, we have real problems in dealing with it on a contemporary and satisfactory basis. But if our constitution represents anything it represents something unique about the country itself on this basis: it seems to me that both in 1867 and in major periods since when we have faced the kind of tensions I quoted from the Globe and Mail, the way in which we have resolved some of our essential difficulties-disputes between regions or between
The Constitution
ethnic or language groups-in the final analysis this country stayed together because we believed enough in respecting each other to negotiate, to hold dialogue, and compromise so that we could achieve a continuing measure of health in our national well-being.
I say this because I come from Charlottetown and to the extent that I have been made aware of what happened in Charlottetown and later in Quebec City, I have always been impressed by the fact that unlike our American friends who had to go through a tremendous inner turmoil and bloodshed, we believe in sitting around the conference table and hammering out some consensus about the country we are going to build.
I remember having this described in a very appealing way almost ten years ago, around the time of the centennial celebrations in Charlottetown. The comedy team of Wayne and Shuster produced a musical at the Confederation Centre and they had a song as the theme for the presentation about the Confederation Conference in 1864. I will not sing it because I do not want to burden members this late on a Friday afternoon. The title was "They just sat down in Charlottetown and built themselves a land". The message conveyed in that song, and it was comparing other countries like the United States, was that we in our country in our own way had a desire and obviously an ability to overcome some of the tremendous obstacles that existed, both in terms of the foreign influence of the major country that was developing to the south and the vast regions that were themselves separated by such great territory, much of it uninhabited at the time, and the linguistic and cultural differences that existed.
In spite of all that, as many an historian has quoted, in this highly unnatural and unusual situation the country was born. That is what makes for the kind of unique format and structure in which our constitution exists.
There is a particular irony to the kind of debate we are having today. We are having the debate because of the experiences and the problems that have arisen vis-a-vis a constitutional question and even more with respect to our confederation over the past eight to ten years. However, the man who holds the chief elected office in this country, the Prime Minister, came into that office very much on the basis that he was the one person who understood what federalism was all about. Here was a man who would show us the way to overcome some of the problems that had existed within Canadian confederation. The irony of that particular situation is that from his election as Prime Minister in 1968 up to the motion that our Creditiste friends have put on the order paper today, and I will quote it again, there has been a contrast between the man who was the leading light when it came to understanding the hopes and possibilities of federalism and this motion of his compatriots from the province of Quebec. The motion reads:
That this House condemns the central government for threatening the provinces with a unilaterally imposed patriation of a constitution which is obsolete and no longer responds to the aspirations of Canadians, rather than, as it should, leaving to the provinces the task of drafting a new constitution.

The Constitution
How tragic that our constitutional discussions, which in a sense is what this Canadian confederation is all about, should come to this today. Surely none of us are surprised. From the beginning when the Prime Minister served in the government of the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson in his confrontation with the then premier of Quebec, Daniel Johnson, and since, his approach has not been one-

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because there are others who want to participate. Beginning with the constitutional discussions from 1968 to 1971, the implementation of the War Measures Act, the whole approach to the then social and economic situation in Quebec, the present approach through unilateral patriation, and more recently the election of a government committed to separatism in the province of Quebec to some degree and in total indicate the rigid unilateral, anachronistic and confrontationistic position the Prime Minister has taken with respect to the health of the country itself in terms of its several peoples, regions and provinces.
What is obviously crucial for us now is to regain some positive sense of what Canada is all about. We must realize that we have a unique and, in some instances, a very fragile experiment. There are not very many federations of the world that have worked successfully. The Prime Minister mentioned this on previous occasions. In some ways our country is a unique experiment with federalism; vast, bilingual, multicultural, all the epithets you can use. I hope that through this debate and others that will follow we will regain some sense of value of our own worth and pluralism. I hope we will regain a commitment to the inherent worth and desire of fulfilment of all the various regions of this country.
Hon. members will know of the concern that many of us in this House share about the realistic respect for the potential of the various regions of this country, not hoping to achieve some kind of bland uniformity, some carbon copy region for region, but realizing there can be some realization of potential and a full free intercourse between the various provinces and regions if we have respect for one another and are prepared to trust one another in this venture. Essentially, it is a regaining of that sense of trust that this debate is all about.
