Mr. Speaker, first of ail I wish to congratulate wholeheartedly and most sincerely the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) who today presented an extremely important and above all timely motion.
The presentation of the hon. member for Shefford is undeniably the most documented and historically the best account of the constitutional past of our country that I have ever heard.

For me, as for the vast majority of my colleagues and Canadians, that account is astounding and unbelievable.
In my turn, Mr. Speaker, in the next few minutes I should like to deal more specifically with the maze of federal and provincial jurisdictions we know and live with at the present time. As the hon. member for Shefford so ably demonstrated, no country in the world has as complex and anarchistic a constitution as Canada.
The constitutional past of our country and its constitutional situation can be aptly defined by the popular rural expression: a cow couldn't find its calf in it.
In practically every field the double jurisdiction has produced confusion and generates problems in almost every sector of economic endeavour. Let us take the official languages for instance. The British North America Act barely mentions the use of languages.
Section 133 specifies that English and French can be used in the debates at the federal level and in Quebec. However, section 133 does not provide sufficient guarantees for the rights of French-speaking and English-speaking minorities. Now, the federal government passed the Official Languages Act in 1969 to guarantee English and French-speakers, whenever this is justified in terms of numbers the right to be served in their mother tongue.
In addition, the Federal Public Service should include the same percentages of English-speaking and French-speaking employees as the population of the country. In 1974, another liberal government, that is in Quebec, passed Bill 22 providing that French was the official language in Quebec. However, eight provinces have no legislation on official languages which means indeed that they do not really have their own Bill 22.
Mr. Speaker, the most recent problem of dual jurisdiction in the matter of Official Languages occured with the pilots' dispute and I was one of the first members to call the attention of this House to this problem. The liberal government, particularly the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), has changed policies at least twice, or once a month, disregarding however the Canadian Official Languages Act.
This is sheer confusion, Mr. Speaker, because we are unable to solve a federal jurisdiction problem about interprovincial transportation. So the Quebec government supported the French-speaking pilots, because under Bill 22 of the Quebec National Assembly, French is the official language in Quebec, since the British North America Act is not clear on languages in Canada.
Let me now turn to the area of general communications. This is another major problem. When the BNA was enacted in 1867, there was of course no television and no radio. So there could not be any provision for either federal or provincial jurisdiction. Since 1930, there has been a major conflict between the federal government and the provinces in matters of communication. This problem is still unsolved, because it is first and foremost a cultural problem.
In French Canada, television and radio are extremely important tools to protect, promote and preserve French cul-
December 3, 1976

ture. The Federal government and the Quebec government are still fighting over this new communications problem, no reference of which ever appeared in the BNA. On the English speaking side, communications are an extremely sensitive issue, because there is a justified fear of Americanization. Therefore communications in Canada must be increasing and entirely Canadian. The Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments, for instance, want to regulate their own communications, particularly cable TV, as does Quebec.
Agriculture is another sore issue between federal and provincial governments. Suffice to recall the war about chickens and eggs that took place between Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba five yeas ago. Quebec tried to limit the import of eggs to protect its own producers when Ontario and Manitoba were shipping the bulk of their egg production to Quebec. But at the same time these two provinces were buying a great many chickens from Quebec and as a reprisal they decided to limit their imports. Yet, chickens and eggs are both products of the same hen are they not?
But the Supreme Court of Canada settled this war about chickens and eggs-which had become a real omelette-by saying the limitation of interprovincial imports was under federal government jurisdiction. British North America Act section 95 states that agriculture is subject to shared jurisdiction, but the conflict over eggs and chickens was caused exactly by this shared jurisdiction. The same thing happened in June 1976 with Quebec milk producers, this time shared jurisdiction over taxation. Once again, another problem occurred because of dual jurisdiction. Under section 92 each province may impose direct taxation within the province while at the same time the federal government may also impose any form of taxation.
This is obviously another case of dual direct taxation in Canada. This is the result of the mess now existing in the financial system: the provinces cannot levy enough direct taxes to pay for the program they are allowed to establish or meet their obligations under the British North America Act, and which are their exclusive jurisdiction.
Consequently, the provinces must get subsidies from the federal government to pay for provincial programs, including education which is, according to section 93 of the British North America Act, exclusively a matter of provincial jurisdiction. Why do we see greater centralization by the federal government and why are the provinces gradually losing their autonomy to the federal government?
Dual jurisdiction over taxation led us directly to dual jurisdiction over matters which are well specified in the British North America Act as coming under provincial jurisdiction. I should like to give an example to make my point. The federal government gives grants to universities which come under provincial jurisdiction. It can therefore through grants control university spending. As a result, the provinces lost some control over universities because of the dual jurisdiction over direct taxation. Under section 92, municipal affairs come
The Constitution
within provincial jurisdiction. Come on, there is already a minister of State for Urban Affairs in Ottawa! This government has managed once again to establish a dual jurisdiction by trying to settle the problem of cities under certain circumstances that are determined by the federal government.
Immigration is one of the most serious issues due to the dual jurisdiction. However, the British North America Act says that federal legislation on immigration takes precedence over provincial legislation, but at the same time immigration is also a matter of economy and culture.
Until recently, most immigrants with special qualifications, such as physicians or engineers, settled down in big cities, where their training is least required. Whereas, at the same time, a lot of Canadian villages have lost their physicians, who were never replaced. And because of this double jurisdiction over immigration, the talents of these immigrants are not used where they are the most urgently needed and could be used most profitably.
The cultural aspect is another issue. It is desirable that immigrants, whatever their place of origin, be able to preserve part of their native culture while living in this country. But, in most cases, immigrants must work in the language of the majority of the area where they are living in Canada. Therefore, it is very important that immigrants in French speaking areas should be prepared to learn French as the language of communication, work and trade.
The problem arising over the double jurisdiction in this area is that in the past, the federal government did do enough to ensure that newcomers to French speaking areas would have the opportunity to learn French. In August 1976, a white paper on the Bank Act was issued by the Minister of Finance.
One of the suggestions made in this document is that the federal government and the Bank of Canada will now have much more control over trust companies and credit unions than in the past. But most of these companies come within provincial jurisdiction. It is obvious therefore, Mr. Speaker, that there will be a fight over dual jurisdiction in 1977, when the Bank is reviewed. Section 91 of the British North America Act stipulates that trade is under federal jurisdiction. But the fact that the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in 1920 that trade came under provincial jurisdiction has led to the terrible state in which trade and industry are now in Canada.
For example, 30 years ago, the textile industry was very strong in Canada and produced all the textiles for our own consumption and even some for exportation. What happened? Once again, because of double jurisdiction, no government in Canada had enough power to ensure the survival of this vital industry and several textile manufacturers went out of business, one after the other, and many workers became unemployed, and the number of unemployed textile workers continues to increase every day, while Canada is importing more and more textile products.
The same thing is happening in the footwear industry, the oldest industry in Canada. Canada needs to determine the

December 3, 1976
The Constitution
specific jurisdiction concerning trade to better protect its industries. The problems of jurisdiction as concerns trade and agriculture are closely related because in many constituencies, trade depends directly on agriculture and of farm products.
There are many other ridiculous examples of federal action in various production areas. For instance, even though beef producers have problems selling their products in Canada, the country imports beef from Australia. If the jurisdictions as concerns trade and agriculture were better defined, these problems could easily be solved. Instead of solving problems of federal and provincial jurisdiction, and of doing something to better distribute power, we let the farmers starve. We let businesses go bankrupt and the other social classes lose ground because of the bureaucratic intervention of the federal government which wants to control everything and to decide nothing.
The control of Western natural resources is another very important problem caused by a double jurisdiction of powers that the federal government set up and imposed. Before 1930, the federal government had control over the natural resources of Alberta and Manitoba. After the thirties these three provinces were given the same rights as the other provinces over their natural resources. Section 92 of the British North America Act states that land, forest and property come under provincial jurisdiction, which means that the large oil reserves of Alberta belong to the province. However, oil is something very important to the country's economy and here again the federal government wants control by regulating the distribution price of Alberta oil, thus creating a new problem of double jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, I could carry on my analysis of the federal-provincial relations in many other areas to demonstrate that this double jurisdiction of powers is paralyzing everyone and creating enormous problems for all the provinces and all the governments because of the complexity of the situation and the ridiculous things that can happen. For instance, milk from the same cow can go partly to Ottawa and partly to Quebec. That is if half the processed milk is used to make fresh milk, that kind of milk comes under provincial jurisdiction. On the other hand, if the other half is used to make industrial milk products, that milk comes under federal jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, if the current pseudo-constitution has not yet created enough problems for everyone, I sincerely believe that it can hardly cause more. Even if in the past we have had problems, we have been living side by for over 100 years; we should be reasonable and serious enough to go on living side by side, as neighbours, in mutual understanding and harmony.
I prefer neighbours with different cultures who get along well to brothers who kill one another. So, Mr. Speaker, like my colleague from Shefford, I ask for a new constitution that would put an end to all those federal-provincial quarrels and that administrative nonsense which are paralyzing everyone as well as the economic development in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, looking at the clock, I realize that I shall not have time to say everything I would like to say as I should have been pleased to use my 20 minutes this afternoon to talk to this very important motion.
In view of the circumstances and the remarks made by hon. members this afternoon, I realize that if many would like to take the floor on that subject, there have been only a few, apart from the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), who made a valuable contribution to the debate this afternoon as nobody really made concrete recommendations or expressed concern about our present constitution. As I have only a few minutes at my disposal, I shall sum up my comments in two points.

Two major points appear to arise out of the proposal currently being made by many of my colleagues in regard to the constitution. One of the first points is the desirability of securing as flexible an amending formula as possible for the constitution, and it should be noted that this has been the objective of successive federal governments since the matter was first raised at the first ministers' conference in the year 1927.
Prior to the period of constitutional review from 1968 to 1971, all attempts to devise a flexible amending formula failed. Even the Fulton-Favreau formula worked out between 1960 and 1964 retained the principle of unanimity for all amendments respecting provincial legislative powers, provincial rights and privileges, provincial assets or property, and the use of the English and French language. The formula devised during the period of constitutional review had and has two great assets; it was agreed to by all first ministers prior to the Victoria conference in the year 1971; and it was the most flexible formula devised in the history of this exercise.
The Victoria formula, which is the basis of the current discussion on the patriation of the British North America Act, gets away for the first time from the principle of unanimity and that of complete rigidity. Rather it provides for regional vetoes on fundamental amendments. A veto can be exercised by any two of the Atlantic provinces, or by Quebec, by Ontario, or by any two of the western provinces having at least 50 per cent of the population of the western provinces.
